The acquisition of new knowledge is significantly influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge, with relevant new knowledge being integrated more efficiently than completely new knowledge.
The evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization, each marked by unique structural and behavioral characteristics.
The evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern, where mid-to-deeper layers first develop the extraction function, and later, lower layers enrich their knowledge representations.
The performance of knowledge circuits is positively correlated with knowledge frequency, with low-frequency knowledge circuits suffering from insufficient representations rather than fundamental capacity limitations.
The state of knowledge circuits could serve as a valuable tracking status for the continual pre-training process, enabling more informed adjustments to training.
future_direction: Utilizing data curriculums in continual pre-training to mimic the structure of the original corpus for more efficient integration.
Using the state of knowledge circuits as a tracking status to enable informed adjustments to training methods or data in response to different phases.
Further investigation into knowledge capacity scaling laws and their impact on model behavior during continual pre-training.
papers.abstract: Despite exceptional capabilities in knowledge-intensive tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) face a critical gap in understanding how they internalize new knowledge, particularly how to structurally embed acquired knowledge in their neural computations. We address this issue through the lens of knowledge circuit evolution, identifying computational subgraphs that facilitate knowledge storage and processing. Our systematic analysis of circuit evolution throughout continual pre-training reveals several key findings: (1) the acquisition of new knowledge is influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge; (2) the evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization; (3) the evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern. These insights not only advance our theoretical understanding of the mechanisms of new knowledge acquisition in LLMs, but also provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance. Code and data will be available at https://github.com/zjunlp/DynamicKnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: On the Behavior of Convolutional Nets for Feature Extraction
papers.research_question: How discriminative are individual CNN features for characterizing classes across different datasets, and how can they be used for knowledge representation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a statistical analysis of individual CNN features for feature extraction, showing that features can be discriminative by both their presence and absence, and that convolutional features are more general and discriminant than previously thought, enabling their use for knowledge representation without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: CNN features, especially from convolutional layers, are highly discriminative and can be used for knowledge representation by both presence and absence, with context being key in the feature extraction process.
papers.key_findings:
Features can be characteristic of a class by their presence or their absence, providing two modalities of information.
Convolutional features are more general and discriminant than previously considered, opening their use for knowledge representation and unsupervised learning.
Low and middle level features behave similarly across datasets, indicating they can be used for knowledge representation on a wide variety of datasets without fine-tuning.
The relevance of fully-connected features is strongly tied to the similarity between the source and target tasks; for dissimilar tasks, they behave similarly to convolutional features.
A thresholding method based on statistical distance can be applied to remove noisy features, with the threshold correlated to the number of images per class.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are representation learning techniques. During training, a deep net is capable of generating a descriptive language of unprecedented size and detail in machine learning. Extracting the descriptive language coded within a trained CNN model (in the case of image data), and reusing it for other purposes is a field of interest, as it provides access to the visual descriptors previously learnt by the CNN after processing millions of images, without requiring an expensive training phase. Contributions to this field (commonly known as feature representation transfer or transfer learning) have been purely empirical so far, extracting all CNN features from a single layer close to the output and testing their performance by feeding them to a classifier. This approach has provided consistent results, although its relevance is limited to classification tasks. In a completely different approach, in this paper we statistically measure the discriminative power of every single feature found within a deep CNN, when used for characterizing every class of 11 datasets. We seek to provide new insights into the behavior of CNN features, particularly the ones from convolutional layers, as this can be relevant for their application to knowledge representation and reasoning. Our results confirm that low and middle level features may behave differently to high level features, but only under certain conditions. We find that all CNN features can be used for knowledge representation purposes both by their presence or by their absence, doubling the information a single CNN feature may provide. We also study how much noise these features may include, and propose a thresholding approach to discard most of it. All these insights have a direct application to the generation of CNN embedding spaces.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Emergent Visual-Semantic Hierarchies in Image-Text Representations
papers.research_question: Do vision-language foundation models exhibit emergent understanding of visual-semantic hierarchies, and how can we probe and enhance this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Foundation vision-language models exhibit emergent hierarchical understanding, and the proposed Radial Embedding framework can probe and enhance this understanding via text-only fine-tuning while retaining pretraining knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Foundation VLMs possess emergent hierarchical knowledge, and the RE framework can reveal and enhance this knowledge, enabling better hierarchical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation VLMs show zero-shot hierarchical understanding, outperforming prior models designed for hierarchy.
The Radial Embedding framework effectively probes hierarchical geometry in VLM embeddings.
Fine-tuning with RE loss improves hierarchical understanding without forgetting pretraining knowledge.
The HierarCaps dataset serves as a benchmark for hierarchical multimodal understanding.
papers.limitation: The automatically generated HierarCaps dataset may contain noise due to limitations of the language model and text-only pipeline.
papers.abstract: While recent vision-and-language models (VLMs) like CLIP are a powerful tool for analyzing text and images in a shared semantic space, they do not explicitly model the hierarchical nature of the set of texts which may describe an image. Conversely, existing multimodal hierarchical representation learning methods require costly training from scratch, failing to leverage the knowledge encoded by state-of-the-art multimodal foundation models. In this work, we study the knowledge of existing foundation models, finding that they exhibit emergent understanding of visual-semantic hierarchies despite not being directly trained for this purpose. We propose the Radial Embedding (RE) framework for probing and optimizing hierarchical understanding, and contribute the HierarCaps dataset, a benchmark facilitating the study of hierarchical knowledge in image--text representations, constructed automatically via large language models. Our results show that foundation VLMs exhibit zero-shot hierarchical understanding, surpassing the performance of prior models explicitly designed for this purpose. Furthermore, we show that foundation models may be better aligned to hierarchical reasoning via a text-only fine-tuning phase, while retaining pretraining knowledge.

papers.title: Beyond Converging Representations A Philosophical Response on the Interpretation Risks of Scientific Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do scientific foundation models of different modalities, architectures, and training data learn similar internal representations of matter?
papers.core_contribution: Representations learned by nearly sixty scientific foundation models across string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities are highly aligned, and they converge as model performance improves, suggesting a common underlying representation of physical reality.
papers.conclusion: Representational alignment serves as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models, and current models remain limited by training data and inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on different input modalities (e.g., string encodings and 3D coordinates) show significant representational alignment.
As models improve in energy prediction performance, their representations converge towards those of the best-performing models.
Local (CKNNA) and global (dCor) alignment metrics show consistent trends, indicating robust representational similarity.
Intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of embeddings is consistent across models for a given dataset, suggesting a universal low-dimensional structure.
For in-distribution data, high-performing models align closely while weak models diverge; for out-of-distribution data, most models collapse to a low-information representation.
papers.limitation: Today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure.
future_direction: Using representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models.
Tracking the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale.
Selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.
papers.abstract: Machine learning models of vastly different modalities and architectures are being trained to predict the behavior of molecules, materials, and proteins. However, it remains unclear whether they learn similar internal representations of matter. Understanding their latent structure is essential for building scientific foundation models that generalize reliably beyond their training domains. Although representational convergence has been observed in language and vision, its counterpart in the sciences has not been systematically explored. Here, we show that representations learned by nearly sixty scientific models, spanning string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities, are highly aligned across a wide range of chemical systems. Models trained on different datasets have highly similar representations of small molecules, and machine learning interatomic potentials converge in representation space as they improve in performance, suggesting that foundation models learn a common underlying representation of physical reality. We then show two distinct regimes of scientific models: on inputs similar to those seen during training, high-performing models align closely and weak models diverge into local sub-optima in representation space; on vastly different structures from those seen during training, nearly all models collapse onto a low-information representation, indicating that today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure. Our findings establish representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models. More broadly, our work can track the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale, and for selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: Linearity of Relation Decoding in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformer language models represent and decode relational knowledge? Is the decoding process for relations linear?
papers.core_contribution: For a subset of relations, transformer language models decode relational knowledge via a linear transformation on the subject representation, which can be estimated from the model's Jacobian.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models employ linear relational embeddings for a subset of relations, revealing a simple, interpretable, but heterogeneously deployed knowledge representation strategy.
papers.key_findings:
For 48% of the relations tested, the relation decoding is well-approximated by a linear relational embedding (LRE).
LREs can be estimated from the model's Jacobian using a few examples and are causally involved in the model's predictions.
Some relations are not linearly decodable, indicating that LMs use heterogeneous knowledge representation strategies.
The attribute lens, built from LREs, visualizes relational knowledge in intermediate layers and can reveal latent knowledge.
LREs can be used to edit subject representations to control model output, demonstrating causal influence.
papers.limitation:
The dataset only includes 47 relations, limiting the generality of the findings.
Evaluation uses first-token correctness, which may lead to false positives when multiple objects share the same first token.
The dataset assumes a single correct object per subject, but some relations may have multiple correct answers.
future_direction: Extending the method to multi-token objects and relations with multiple correct answers.
Applying LREs to mitigate biases in models.
papers.abstract: Much of the knowledge encoded in transformer language models (LMs) may be expressed in terms of relations: relations between words and their synonyms, entities and their attributes, etc. We show that, for a subset of relations, this computation is well-approximated by a single linear transformation on the subject representation. Linear relation representations may be obtained by constructing a first-order approximation to the LM from a single prompt, and they exist for a variety of factual, commonsense, and linguistic relations. However, we also identify many cases in which LM predictions capture relational knowledge accurately, but this knowledge is not linearly encoded in their representations. Our results thus reveal a simple, interpretable, but heterogeneously deployed knowledge representation strategy in transformer LMs.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1, Knowledge Storage and Extraction
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize knowledge during training, and extract it later to answer questions or perform logical reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling) in pretraining data is crucial for reliable knowledge extraction via instruction fine-tuning, and introduces linear probing techniques to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes with practical recommendations for LLM pretraining: data rewriting (augmentation) is important, and including instruction-like data in pretraining is beneficial.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training (pretraining on both biographies and QA data) enables knowledge extraction, but the model learns in an abnormal way (first from QA then correlates with BIO).
Without knowledge augmentation in pretraining, instruction fine-tuning fails to extract knowledge (0% accuracy).
Knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) during pretraining enables knowledge extraction after fine-tuning.
Linear probing shows that knowledge augmentation causes knowledge to be linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names, whereas without augmentation it is distributed across tokens.
Including celebrity data (with augmentation) in pretraining improves knowledge extraction for minority data (without augmentation).
future_direction: Studying logical reasoning and knowledge manipulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a vast amount of world knowledge, often extractable via question-answering (e.g., "What is Abraham Lincoln's birthday?"). However, do they answer such questions based on exposure to similar questions during training (i.e., cheating), or by genuinely learning to extract knowledge from sources like Wikipedia? In this paper, we investigate this issue using a controlled biography dataset. We find a strong correlation between the model's ability to extract knowledge and various diversity measures of the training data. $\textbf{Essentially}$, for knowledge to be reliably extracted, it must be sufficiently augmented (e.g., through paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) $\textit{during pretraining}$. Without such augmentation, knowledge may be memorized but not extractable, leading to 0% accuracy, regardless of subsequent instruction fine-tuning. To understand why this occurs, we employ (nearly) linear probing to demonstrate a strong connection between the observed correlation and how the model internally encodes knowledge -- whether it is linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names or distributed across other token embeddings in the training text. This paper provides $\textbf{several key recommendations for LLM pretraining in the industry}$: (1) rewrite the pretraining data -- using small, auxiliary models -- to provide knowledge augmentation, and (2) incorporate more instruction-finetuning data into the pretraining stage before it becomes too late.

papers.title: Interpretable Visual Reasoning via Induced Symbolic Space
papers.research_question: How to induce visual concepts and their hierarchical relationships from question-answer pairs and images, and use them for interpretable visual reasoning.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OCCAM, an object-centric visual reasoning framework that induces symbolic concepts and their hierarchy from question-answer pairs, achieving interpretable reasoning without human-annotated programs.
papers.conclusion: OCCAM achieves state-of-the-art visual reasoning and induces accurate, sufficient concepts for interpretable reasoning, enabling future extension to more sophisticated induction tasks.
papers.key_findings:
OCCAM achieves new state-of-the-art on CLEVR and GQA without external program supervision.
Induced concepts are sufficient for visual reasoning, with only ~1% performance drop when replacing visual features with concepts.
The induced concept hierarchy on CLEVR perfectly matches the data generator definition and human prior knowledge.
papers.limitation: Real-world data makes it difficult to induce some commonsense super concepts due to objects having multiple values for a concept (e.g., colors) and degrees of concepts.
future_direction: Extending concept induction to phrases, more complicated hierarchies, and degrees of features.
papers.abstract: We study the problem of concept induction in visual reasoning, i.e., identifying concepts and their hierarchical relationships from question-answer pairs associated with images; and achieve an interpretable model via working on the induced symbolic concept space. To this end, we first design a new framework named object-centric compositional attention model (OCCAM) to perform the visual reasoning task with object-level visual features. Then, we come up with a method to induce concepts of objects and relations using clues from the attention patterns between objects' visual features and question words. Finally, we achieve a higher level of interpretability by imposing OCCAM on the objects represented in the induced symbolic concept space. Our model design makes this an easy adaption via first predicting the concepts of objects and relations and then projecting the predicted concepts back to the visual feature space so the compositional reasoning module can process normally. Experiments on the CLEVR and GQA datasets demonstrate: 1) our OCCAM achieves a new state of the art without human-annotated functional programs; 2) our induced concepts are both accurate and sufficient as OCCAM achieves an on-par performance on objects represented either in visual features or in the induced symbolic concept space.

papers.title: The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It's Lying
papers.research_question: Can the internal state of an LLM be used to reveal the truthfulness of statements, both provided to and generated by the LLM?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM internal activations contain information about statement truthfulness and introduces SAPLMA, a classifier that uses these activations to detect false statements with higher accuracy than baselines like few-shot prompting.
papers.conclusion: SAPLMA leverages LLM hidden activations to predict statement truthfulness, offering a way to filter false information and increase trust in LLM-generated content.
papers.key_findings:
SAPLMA achieves accuracy between 60% to 80% on specific topics with OPT-6.7b and 70% to 90% with LLAMA2-7b, outperforming few-shot prompting which maxes at 56% accuracy.
The optimal hidden layer for SAPLMA varies between models, e.g., 20th layer for OPT-6.7b and middle layer for LLAMA2-7b.
Sentence probability assigned by the LLM is not a reliable indicator of truthfulness due to dependencies on sentence length and word frequencies.
SAPLMA can classify both externally provided statements and those generated by the LLM itself.
The method does not require fine-tuning the LLM, using only a trained classifier on frozen activations.
papers.limitation:
The method detects binary true/false, but in practice, detecting uncertainty or confidence levels might be more useful.
Tested only in English; applicability to multilingual settings is not verified.
For longer responses, activation values might need decoupling to isolate the most recent statement.
future_direction: Apply SAPLMA to larger LLMs and conduct human interaction experiments.
Study how activations develop over time as additional words are generated.
Extend to multilingual input and test cross-language applicability.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown exceptional performance in various tasks, one of their most prominent drawbacks is generating inaccurate or false information with a confident tone. In this paper, we provide evidence that the LLM's internal state can be used to reveal the truthfulness of statements. This includes both statements provided to the LLM, and statements that the LLM itself generates. Our approach is to train a classifier that outputs the probability that a statement is truthful, based on the hidden layer activations of the LLM as it reads or generates the statement. Experiments demonstrate that given a set of test sentences, of which half are true and half false, our trained classifier achieves an average of 71\% to 83\% accuracy labeling which sentences are true versus false, depending on the LLM base model. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between our classifier's performance and approaches based on the probability assigned to the sentence by the LLM. We show that while LLM-assigned sentence probability is related to sentence truthfulness, this probability is also dependent on sentence length and the frequencies of words in the sentence, resulting in our trained classifier providing a more reliable approach to detecting truthfulness, highlighting its potential to enhance the reliability of LLM-generated content and its practical applicability in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Birds have four legs?! NumerSense: Probing Numerical Commonsense Knowledge of Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: Does and to what extent do pre-trained language models capture numerical commonsense knowledge, and how robust is this knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing task and dataset (NumerSense) to evaluate numerical commonsense knowledge in pre-trained language models, finding that models perform poorly and are brittle to adversarial perturbations.
papers.conclusion: Powerful pre-trained models such as BERT and RoBERTa perform surprisingly poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge even after fine-tuning, and the introduced dataset provides a basis for future improvement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT and RoBERTa perform poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge without fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning with distant supervision improves performance but still far from human performance.
Models are brittle to adversarial examples (e.g., inserting adjectives).
Attention analysis shows that important words for numerical commonsense (subject/object) receive low attention weights.
Open-domain QA models also perform poorly on 'how-many' questions derived from NumerSense.
future_direction: Improving PTLMs' abilities to faithfully capture (numerical) commonsense.
Populating numerical facts in current commonsense knowledge bases.
Improving open-domain QA for 'how-many' questions.
Incorporating more structured inductive biases (e.g., dependencies and semantic roles) in pre-training.
Controlling bias in masked language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent works show that pre-trained language models (PTLMs), such as BERT, possess certain commonsense and factual knowledge. They suggest that it is promising to use PTLMs as "neural knowledge bases" via predicting masked words. Surprisingly, we find that this may not work for numerical commonsense knowledge (e.g., a bird usually has two legs). In this paper, we investigate whether and to what extent we can induce numerical commonsense knowledge from PTLMs as well as the robustness of this process. To study this, we introduce a novel probing task with a diagnostic dataset, NumerSense, containing 13.6k masked-word-prediction probes (10.5k for fine-tuning and 3.1k for testing). Our analysis reveals that: (1) BERT and its stronger variant RoBERTa perform poorly on the diagnostic dataset prior to any fine-tuning; (2) fine-tuning with distant supervision brings some improvement; (3) the best supervised model still performs poorly as compared to human performance (54.06% vs 96.3% in accuracy).

papers.title: Crawling The Internal Knowledge-Base of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we extract a structured knowledge graph representing the factual knowledge encoded in a language model, starting from a single seed entity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a prompt-based method (LMCRAWL) to crawl a knowledge graph from a language model by decomposing the task into relation generation, object generation, and paraphrasing sub-tasks, achieving high precision.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a feasible method for extracting structured knowledge graphs from language models, representing an important step towards making the internal knowledge of LMs interpretable and usable.
papers.key_findings:
The LMCRAWL method achieves high precision (82-92%) in extracting factual triplets from GPT-3.
The number of facts extracted correlates with entity frequency in Wikidata, suggesting the model encodes more knowledge about popular entities.
Using a 'Don't Know' mechanism and paraphrasing improves precision and recall control.
The method can generate facts outside predefined schemas (e.g., Wikidata).
Automatic evaluation via Google search is a conservative estimate, with manual analysis suggesting true precision may be higher.
papers.limitation:
Cost and scalability issues limit the extraction of larger graphs (more hops).
Error propagation can occur when mistakes in early nodes lead to more mistakes in subsequent expansions.
Automatic precision evaluation is approximate and may underestimate true precision.
It is challenging to measure recall or knowledge coverage accurately.
The source of inaccuracies (extraction method vs. model knowledge) is not addressed.
future_direction: Expanding to larger graphs with more hops.
Introducing consistency constraints to increase precision.
Using the extracted knowledge graph as a question-answering mechanism.
papers.abstract: Language models are trained on large volumes of text, and as a result their parameters might contain a significant body of factual knowledge. Any downstream task performed by these models implicitly builds on these facts, and thus it is highly desirable to have means for representing this body of knowledge in an interpretable way. However, there is currently no mechanism for such a representation.Here, we propose to address this goal by extracting a knowledge-graph of facts from a given language model. We describe a procedure for "crawling" the internal knowledge-base of a language model. Specifically, given a seed entity, we expand a knowledge-graph around it. The crawling procedure is decomposed into sub-tasks, realized through specially designed prompts that control for both precision (i.e., that no wrong facts are generated) and recall (i.e., the number of facts generated). We evaluate our approach on graphs crawled starting from dozens of seed entities, and show it yields high precision graphs (82-92%), while emitting a reasonable number of facts per entity.

papers.title: Information Structure in Mappings: An Approach to Learning, Representation, and Generalisation
papers.research_question: How can we describe the structure of representations in neural networks, how does this structure emerge during training, and what kinds of structures enable generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis introduces quantitative methods for identifying systematic structure in mappings between spaces, and leverages them to understand how deep-learning models learn to represent information, what representational structures drive generalisation, and how design decisions condition the structures that emerge. It also introduces a novel, performant approach to estimating the entropy of vector space.
papers.conclusion: The thesis concludes that information structure methods provide insights into how models learn and generalize, drawing parallels between neural networks and human language.
papers.key_findings:
The methods can identify systematic structure in mappings and relate it to generalization.
There are distinct phases of training: early learning of lexical information followed by contextualization.
Model size affects representational structure: larger models develop more robust representations.
Information structure measures can predict downstream performance.
Regularity in representations is important for generalization.
papers.limitation: It’s unclear if the learnability of a language at timestep n matters at n+1 when the language has changed.
future_direction: Further study of the role learnability plays in an emergent context, where what is learned changes, is needed to understand the full picture.
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable success of large large-scale neural networks, we still lack unified notation for thinking about and describing their representational spaces. We lack methods to reliably describe how their representations are structured, how that structure emerges over training, and what kinds of structures are desirable. This thesis introduces quantitative methods for identifying systematic structure in a mapping between spaces, and leverages them to understand how deep-learning models learn to represent information, what representational structures drive generalisation, and how design decisions condition the structures that emerge. To do this I identify structural primitives present in a mapping, along with information theoretic quantifications of each. These allow us to analyse learning, structure, and generalisation across multi-agent reinforcement learning models, sequence-to-sequence models trained on a single task, and Large Language Models. I also introduce a novel, performant, approach to estimating the entropy of vector space, that allows this analysis to be applied to models ranging in size from 1 million to 12 billion parameters. The experiments here work to shed light on how large-scale distributed models of cognition learn, while allowing us to draw parallels between those systems and their human analogs. They show how the structures of language and the constraints that give rise to them in many ways parallel the kinds of structures that drive performance of contemporary neural networks.

papers.title: Representational Systems Theory: A Unified Approach to Encoding, Analysing and Transforming Representations
papers.research_question: How can we develop a unified theoretical framework to encode, analyze, and transform representations across different representational systems?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representational Systems Theory, a unified framework for encoding representations from syntactic, entailment, and property perspectives, and for transforming representations between systems.
papers.conclusion: Representational Systems Theory offers a unified framework for encoding and transforming representations, with potential for widespread application in AI and other fields.
papers.key_findings:
Representational Systems Theory provides a unified encoding of representational systems via construction spaces, capturing grammatical construction, entailment relations, and meta-level properties.
The theory enables representational-system-agnostic transformation algorithms, removing the need for system-specific algorithms.
The approach permits derivation of partial transformations when no terminating algorithm can produce a complete transformation.
future_direction: Development of AI tools that exploit Representational Systems Theory to invoke structural transformations.
Developing a generic model for estimating cognitive costs of representations.
papers.abstract: The study of representations is of fundamental importance to any form of communication, and our ability to exploit them effectively is paramount. This article presents a novel theory -- Representational Systems Theory -- that is designed to abstractly encode a wide variety of representations from three core perspectives: syntax, entailment, and their properties. By introducing the concept of a construction space, we are able to encode each of these core components under a single, unifying paradigm. Using our Representational Systems Theory, it becomes possible to structurally transform representations in one system into representations in another. An intrinsic facet of our structural transformation technique is representation selection based on properties that representations possess, such as their relative cognitive effectiveness or structural complexity. A major theoretical barrier to providing general structural transformation techniques is a lack of terminating algorithms. Representational Systems Theory permits the derivation of partial transformations when no terminating algorithm can produce a full transformation. Since Representational Systems Theory provides a universal approach to encoding representational systems, a further key barrier is eliminated: the need to devise system-specific structural transformation algorithms, that are necessary when different systems adopt different formalisation approaches. Consequently, Representational Systems Theory is the first general framework that provides a unified approach to encoding representations, supports representation selection via structural transformations, and has the potential for widespread practical application.

papers.title: Attention Sinks: A 'Catch, Tag, Release' Mechanism for Embeddings
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why attention sinks emerge in later tokens, whether they encode semantically meaningful information, how they differ between pretrained and reasoning models, and the impact of query-key normalization on attention sinks.
papers.core_contribution: This paper uncovers the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism in LLMs, where attention sinks catch tokens, tag them with semantically meaningful information, and release the tags into the residual stream for later use. The mechanism is prevalent across model families, more pronounced in reasoning models, and persists despite query-key normalization.
papers.conclusion: This work uncovers and formalizes the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism mediated by attention sinks, showing that sinks implement a functional tagging system that propagates semantically meaningful information across tokens, offering a foundation for deeper mechanistic investigations.
papers.key_findings:
Attention sinks implement a 'catch, tag, release' mechanism, where sinks catch tokens, tag them with a common direction, and release the tags into the residual stream.
Tags encode semantically meaningful information, such as the truth value of statements, as shown by probing experiments.
Reasoning-distilled models exhibit the mechanism more strongly, with more attention sinks and higher variance explained by tags.
Attention sinks remain prevalent in models with query-key normalization, despite the normalization's intended effect.
The mechanism can emerge through training in a minimal theoretical model designed to solve a sequence averaging task.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical model does not prove the mechanism is necessary and may not reflect real-world complexity.
The threshold-based metric for identifying attention sinks may not capture all such tokens and lacks a principled method for setting the threshold.
The connection between the mechanism and reasoning is suggestive but not causally established.
future_direction: Deeper mechanistic investigations into token interactions and the role of implicit memory in transformers.
Establishing a causal link between the mechanism and reasoning.
Exploring practical applications such as steering activations for alignment and safety, and preserving the mechanism in model compression.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often concentrate their attention on a few specific tokens referred to as attention sinks. Common examples include the first token, a prompt-independent sink, and punctuation tokens, which are prompt-dependent. While the tokens causing the sinks often lack direct semantic meaning, the presence of the sinks is critical for model performance, particularly under model compression and KV-caching. Despite their ubiquity, the function, semantic role, and origin of attention sinks -- especially those beyond the first token -- remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation demonstrating that attention sinks: catch a sequence of tokens, tag them using a common direction in embedding space, and release them back into the residual stream, where tokens are later retrieved based on the tags they have acquired. Probing experiments reveal these tags carry semantically meaningful information, such as the truth of a statement. These findings extend to reasoning models, where the mechanism spans more heads and explains greater variance in embeddings, or recent models with query-key normalization, where sinks remain just as prevalent. To encourage future theoretical analysis, we introduce a minimal problem which can be solved through the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism, and where it emerges through training.

papers.title: Internal knowledge representation on trainer agents by using interactive reinforcement learning
papers.research_question: What internal representation and characteristics of artificial trainer-agents determine which agent is a better advisor in interactive reinforcement learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in interactive reinforcement learning, trainer agents with homogeneously distributed experience (polymath agents) are better advisors than those with high reward but limited knowledge (fast agents), due to more complete internal knowledge representation.
papers.conclusion: Polymath agents, with homogeneously distributed experience, have more complete internal knowledge representation and are therefore better advisors for other RL agents compared to fast agents with high reward but incomplete knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fast agents accumulate more reward but have incomplete knowledge in states not on the shortest path.
Polymath agents have homogeneously distributed experience and explore multiple paths.
Accumulating high reward does not necessarily make an agent a good trainer.
Internal Q-value heat maps reveal uniform regions in fast agents indicating no preferred action in some states.
Polymath agents have more complete internal knowledge representation and are better candidates for advisors.
papers.abstract: Interactive reinforcement learning has become an important apprenticeship approach to speed up convergence in classic reinforcement learning problems. On some occasions, the trainer may be another artificial agent which in turn was trained using reinforcement learning methods to afterward become an advisor for other learner-agents. In this work, we analyze internal representation and characteristics of artificial trainer-agents to determine which agent may outperform others to become a better advisor.

papers.title: Do LLMs Know about Hallucination? An Empirical Investigation of LLM's Hidden States
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess awareness of hallucination, and if so, to what extent and through what mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that LLMs exhibit awareness of hallucination through differences in hidden states when processing correct vs hallucinated answers, and shows potential for using hidden state guidance to mitigate hallucination.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess awareness of hallucination as evidenced by differences in hidden states, and leveraging hidden state guidance can help mitigate hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
LLM’s final hidden state is more susceptible to be influenced by a correct answer compared to a hallucinated one.
Strategically inducing an LLM to produce hallucinated responses can raise its awareness consequently.
The level of awareness corresponds to the uncertainty of the LLM in the responses.
Providing relevant knowledge can assist LLMs in identifying hallucinated responses.
The transition between hidden states encodes truthfulness information.
papers.limitation:
Do not differentiate between fine-grained categories of hallucination.
Do not examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers, only the final layer.
Experiments are performed on conventional QA tasks, not more complicated or domain-specific tasks.
Future research is needed to develop more effective strategies for mitigating LLM hallucination.
future_direction: Explore different types of hallucination (factual fabrication, instruction inconsistency, etc.).
Examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers and investigate layer-by-layer formation of hallucination.
Adapt the experimental framework to more complicated or domain-specific tasks and potentially extend to multimodal features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make up answers that are not real, and this is known as hallucination. This research aims to see if, how, and to what extent LLMs are aware of hallucination. More specifically, we check whether and how an LLM reacts differently in its hidden states when it answers a question right versus when it hallucinates. To do this, we introduce an experimental framework which allows examining LLM's hidden states in different hallucination situations. Building upon this framework, we conduct a series of experiments with language models in the LLaMA family (Touvron et al., 2023). Our empirical findings suggest that LLMs react differently when processing a genuine response versus a fabricated one. We then apply various model interpretation techniques to help understand and explain the findings better. Moreover, informed by the empirical observations, we show great potential of using the guidance derived from LLM's hidden representation space to mitigate hallucination. We believe this work provides insights into how LLMs produce hallucinated answers and how to make them occur less often.

papers.title: Multi-Neuron Representations of Hierarchical Concepts in Spiking Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can hierarchical concepts be represented in spiking neural networks to support fault-tolerant recognition when partial information is presented and neurons may fail?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces multi-neuron representations of hierarchical concepts in spiking neural networks for fault-tolerant recognition under partial information and neuron failures, with probabilistic analysis of recognition success.
papers.conclusion: Multi-neuron representations enable fault-tolerant recognition of hierarchical concepts in spiking neural networks under partial information and neuron failures, with analysis providing probabilistic guarantees.
papers.key_findings:
Recognition works correctly in three types of spiking neural networks with high probability, depending on the number of representative neurons and the neuron failure probability.
The probability of correct recognition increases with the number of representatives and decreases with the failure probability.
Representations using multiple neurons per concept provide redundancy and fault tolerance.
Learning algorithms for these representations are discussed, inspired by prior work on Hebbian learning and assembly calculus.
papers.limitation:
Strong uniformity assumptions, such as all concepts having the same number of children and neurons failing independently with the same probability.
The analysis may not yield the tightest possible bounds.
The model omits feedback edges and considers only initial random failures.
future_direction: Simulating the algorithms to evaluate performance and improve analysis.
Extending the failure model to include online failures.
Incorporating feedback edges into the network model.
Completing the analysis of the proposed learning algorithms, especially for networks with lateral edges.
papers.abstract: We describe how hierarchical concepts can be represented in three types of layered neural networks. The aim is to support recognition of the concepts when partial information about the concepts is presented, and also when some of the neurons in the network might fail. Our failure model involves initial random failures. The three types of networks are: feed-forward networks with high connectivity, feed-forward networks with low connectivity, and layered networks with low connectivity and with both forward edges and "lateral" edges within layers. In order to achieve fault-tolerance, the representations all use multiple representative neurons for each concept. We show how recognition can work in all three of these settings, and quantify how the probability of correct recognition depends on several parameters, including the number of representatives and the neuron failure probability. We also discuss how these representations might be learned, in all three types of networks. For the feed-forward networks, the learning algorithms are similar to ones used in [4], whereas for networks with lateral edges, the algorithms are generally inspired by work on the assembly calculus [3, 6, 7].

papers.title: Revealing emergent human-like conceptual representations from language prediction
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) develop human-like concepts through language prediction, and how such concepts are represented, organized, and linked to behavior.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that structured, human-like conceptual representations can emerge in LLMs purely from language prediction, without real-world grounding. These representations converge to a shared, context-independent structure that predicts model performance and aligns with human behavioral and neural data.
papers.conclusion: The findings establish that critical aspects of human conceptual representation and organization can emerge purely from language prediction in LLMs, offering a tractable window into human concepts and advancing alignment between artificial and human intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can flexibly derive concepts from definitional descriptions using in-context learning, with performance improving with more demonstrations.
The conceptual representations formed by LLMs converge toward a shared, context-independent relational structure as the number of contextual demonstrations increases.
Alignment of a model's conceptual representations with this convergent structure reliably predicts its performance on a range of language understanding and reasoning tasks.
LLM-derived conceptual representations effectively predict human behavioral judgments, such as similarity ratings and categorization, outperforming static word embeddings.
The convergent conceptual representations align closely with neural activity patterns in the human brain, providing evidence for their biological plausibility.
papers.limitation: LLMs struggled to predict human judgments when they relied on perceptual properties like color or texture, indicating a divergence from human judgments in visually grounded dimensions.
papers.abstract: People acquire concepts through rich physical and social experiences and use them to understand and navigate the world. In contrast, large language models (LLMs), trained solely through next-token prediction on text, exhibit strikingly human-like behaviors. Are these models developing concepts akin to those of humans? If so, how are such concepts represented, organized, and related to behavior? Here, we address these questions by investigating the representations formed by LLMs during an in-context concept inference task. We found that LLMs can flexibly derive concepts from linguistic descriptions in relation to contextual cues about other concepts. The derived representations converge toward a shared, context-independent structure, and alignment with this structure reliably predicts model performance across various understanding and reasoning tasks. Moreover, the convergent representations effectively capture human behavioral judgments and closely align with neural activity patterns in the human brain, providing evidence for biological plausibility. Together, these findings establish that structured, human-like conceptual representations can emerge purely from language prediction without real-world grounding, highlighting the role of conceptual structure in understanding intelligent behavior. More broadly, our work suggests that LLMs offer a tangible window into the nature of human concepts and lays the groundwork for advancing alignment between artificial and human intelligence.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: The Evolution of Representation in Simple Cognitive Networks
papers.research_question: How are representations developed in cognitive systems, and are they necessary for intelligent behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an information-theoretic measure of representation (R) and shows that the capacity to represent increases during evolutionary adaptation in simple cognitive networks.
papers.conclusion: The measure R can quantify representations in any cognitive system and should be predictive of an agent's long-term adaptive success.
papers.key_findings:
The representation measure R increases during evolutionary adaptation in both artificial neural networks and Markov brains.
Markov brains evolve to become less dependent on sensory inputs and more dependent on internal states than artificial neural networks.
Networks form representations of specific environmental features (concepts) and these representations are distributed across nodes.
Representations are formed over the lifetime of the agent, building up as the agent integrates information.
The evolved networks can be analyzed to determine which nodes represent which environmental features.
future_direction: Future investigations on what kind of system is more powerful for making intelligent decisions using representations.
papers.abstract: Representations are internal models of the environment that can provide guidance to a behaving agent, even in the absence of sensory information. It is not clear how representations are developed and whether they are necessary or even essential for intelligent behavior. We argue here that the ability to represent relevant features of the environment is the expected consequence of an adaptive process, give a formal definition of representation based on information theory, and quantify it with a measure R. To measure how R changes over time, we evolve two types of networks--an artificial neural network and a network of hidden Markov gates--to solve a categorization task using a genetic algorithm. We find that the capacity to represent increases during evolutionary adaptation and that agents form representations of their environment during their lifetime. This ability allows the agents to act on sensorial inputs in the context of their acquired representations and enables complex and context-dependent behavior. We examine which concepts (features of the environment) our networks are representing, how the representations are logically encoded in the networks, and how they form as an agent behaves to solve a task. We conclude that R should be able to quantify the representations within any cognitive system and should be predictive of an agent's long-term adaptive success.

papers.title: Bilinear relational structure fixes reversal curse and enables consistent model editing
papers.research_question: Is the reversal curse an inherent limitation of language models, and can it be mitigated by learning a bilinear relational structure in internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The reversal curse and model editing failures are not inherent but stem from unstructured knowledge representations; training with appropriate regularization induces a bilinear relational structure that mitigates the curse and enables logically consistent editing.
papers.conclusion: The reversal curse and editing generalization failures are symptoms of unstructured internal knowledge representations; inducing bilinear relational geometry through training and regularization leads to more reliable and editable language models.
papers.key_findings:
Weight decay regularization enables models to overcome the reversal curse by learning a more generalizable internal structure.
Successful models develop a robust bilinear relational structure in their hidden representations, peaking in middle layers.
The learned bilinear matrices obey algebraic properties (inversion via transpose, composition via product), enabling multi-hop inference.
Models with bilinear structure successfully propagate single-fact edits to logically entailed facts (reverse and neighborhood relations).
A strong positive correlation exists between a model's bilinear probe accuracy and its logical generalization performance after editing.
papers.limitation: The study uses language models trained from scratch on a clean, synthetic dataset, which may not scale to large, pre-trained language models with noisy, complex knowledge.
future_direction: Investigate whether similar bilinear structures exist in large-scale pre-trained language models.
Develop geometry-aware editing algorithms that leverage internal relational structures.
Explore 'architectural preparation' strategies to endow models with structured knowledge representations during pre-training or fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The reversal curse -- a language model's (LM) inability to infer an unseen fact ``B is A'' from a learned fact ``A is B'' -- is widely considered a fundamental limitation. We show that this is not an inherent failure but an artifact of how models encode knowledge. By training LMs from scratch on a synthetic dataset of relational knowledge graphs, we demonstrate that bilinear relational structure emerges in their hidden representations. This structure substantially alleviates the reversal curse, enabling LMs to infer unseen reverse facts. Crucially, we also find that this bilinear structure plays a key role in consistent model editing. When a fact is updated in a LM with this structure, the edit correctly propagates to its reverse and other logically dependent facts. In contrast, models lacking this representation not only suffer from the reversal curse but also fail to generalize edits, further introducing logical inconsistencies. Our results establish that training on a relational knowledge dataset induces the emergence of bilinear internal representations, which in turn enable LMs to behave in a logically consistent manner after editing. This implies that the success of model editing depends critically not just on editing algorithms but on the underlying representational geometry of the knowledge being modified.

papers.title: Analysing the Residual Stream of Language Models Under Knowledge Conflicts
papers.research_question: Can we identify the conflict between context and parameter knowledge by probing the residual stream? Can we know which source of knowledge the models will use before they generate the answers?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally register knowledge conflict signals in the residual stream, which can be detected by probing intermediate activations. The residual stream shows distinct skewness patterns when the model relies on contextual versus parametric knowledge, enabling prediction of the model's knowledge selection behavior.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit internal mechanisms for identifying conflicts in the mid-layers, and the residual stream shows distinct skewness patterns when the model uses context and parametric knowledge to predict. This analysis provides insights into the behaviour of LLMs in the presence of knowledge conflicts.
papers.key_findings:
The signal of knowledge conflict rises from intermediate layers (e.g., layer 13-14) and can be detected with high accuracy using linear probing.
The residual stream exhibits different skewness patterns (measured by Kurtosis, Hoyer, Gini) when the model uses contextual knowledge versus parametric knowledge.
The decision of which knowledge to use occurs after the detection of the knowledge conflict signal.
The probing model's performance for conflict detection peaks around the 14th layer and then decreases slightly.
The skewness patterns are more pronounced in hidden states than in MLP or Self-Attention activations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a significant amount of factual knowledge in their parameters. However, their parametric knowledge may conflict with the information provided in the context. Such conflicts can lead to undesirable model behaviour, such as reliance on outdated or incorrect information. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can identify knowledge conflicts and whether it is possible to know which source of knowledge the model will rely on by analysing the residual stream of the LLM. Through probing tasks, we find that LLMs can internally register the signal of knowledge conflict in the residual stream, which can be accurately detected by probing the intermediate model activations. This allows us to detect conflicts within the residual stream before generating the answers without modifying the input or model parameters. Moreover, we find that the residual stream shows significantly different patterns when the model relies on contextual knowledge versus parametric knowledge to resolve conflicts. This pattern can be employed to estimate the behaviour of LLMs when conflict happens and prevent unexpected answers before producing the answers. Our analysis offers insights into how LLMs internally manage knowledge conflicts and provides a foundation for developing methods to control the knowledge selection processes.

papers.title: Trees in transformers: a theoretical analysis of the Transformer's ability to represent trees
papers.research_question: Can Transformer networks capture tree structures, what are the limits of this ability, and how can the learning process be made more efficient?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves theoretically that a 1-layer Transformer can find tree backbone vectors and that two linear layers with ReLU can recover any tree backbone from two linearly independent starting backbones, and empirically shows standard Transformers can learn tree structures, albeit with slower convergence than when tree position is explicitly encoded.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can capture tree structures; a 1-layer 1-head Transformer can handle trees within its input length limit, but a 2-layer Transformer is necessary to learn all possible tree backbones, and learning efficiency can be improved by explicitly encoding tree structure information.
papers.key_findings:
A 1-layer, 1 attention head Transformer can find the backbone vector for any tree (Proposition 1).
Two linear layers with ReLU activation can recover any tree backbone from any two nonzero, linearly independent starting backbones (Theorem 1).
Standard Transformers achieve similar accuracy compared to Transformers with explicit tree position encoding, but with slower convergence.
Transformers can learn tree structures in practice, as shown by synthetic experiments.
Explicit tree positional encodings lead to faster convergence and sometimes higher accuracy in tree transduction tasks.
papers.limitation: Experiments are conducted on synthetic data, so generalization to real-world data is unclear.
future_direction: Further (computationally intensive) experiments to understand the asymptotic boundary of how much tree information benefits training.
Investigating deeper networks or more training steps for hard tasks like parent12 and parent123.
papers.abstract: Transformer networks are the de facto standard architecture in natural language processing. To date, there are no theoretical analyses of the Transformer's ability to capture tree structures. We focus on the ability of Transformer networks to learn tree structures that are important for tree transduction problems. We first analyze the theoretical capability of the standard Transformer architecture to learn tree structures given enumeration of all possible tree backbones, which we define as trees without labels. We then prove that two linear layers with ReLU activation function can recover any tree backbone from any two nonzero, linearly independent starting backbones. This implies that a Transformer can learn tree structures well in theory. We conduct experiments with synthetic data and find that the standard Transformer achieves similar accuracy compared to a Transformer where tree position information is explicitly encoded, albeit with slower convergence. This confirms empirically that Transformers can learn tree structures.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
