papers.research_question: What internal representation and characteristics of artificial trainer-agents determine which agent is a better advisor in interactive reinforcement learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in interactive reinforcement learning, trainer agents with homogeneously distributed experience (polymath agents) are better advisors than those with high reward but limited knowledge (fast agents), due to more complete internal knowledge representation.
papers.conclusion: Polymath agents, with homogeneously distributed experience, have more complete internal knowledge representation and are therefore better advisors for other RL agents compared to fast agents with high reward but incomplete knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fast agents accumulate more reward but have incomplete knowledge in states not on the shortest path.
Polymath agents have homogeneously distributed experience and explore multiple paths.
Accumulating high reward does not necessarily make an agent a good trainer.
Internal Q-value heat maps reveal uniform regions in fast agents indicating no preferred action in some states.
Polymath agents have more complete internal knowledge representation and are better candidates for advisors.
papers.abstract: Interactive reinforcement learning has become an important apprenticeship approach to speed up convergence in classic reinforcement learning problems. On some occasions, the trainer may be another artificial agent which in turn was trained using reinforcement learning methods to afterward become an advisor for other learner-agents. In this work, we analyze internal representation and characteristics of artificial trainer-agents to determine which agent may outperform others to become a better advisor.

papers.title: Do LLMs Know about Hallucination? An Empirical Investigation of LLM's Hidden States
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess awareness of hallucination, and if so, to what extent and through what mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that LLMs exhibit awareness of hallucination through differences in hidden states when processing correct vs hallucinated answers, and shows potential for using hidden state guidance to mitigate hallucination.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess awareness of hallucination as evidenced by differences in hidden states, and leveraging hidden state guidance can help mitigate hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
LLM’s final hidden state is more susceptible to be influenced by a correct answer compared to a hallucinated one.
Strategically inducing an LLM to produce hallucinated responses can raise its awareness consequently.
The level of awareness corresponds to the uncertainty of the LLM in the responses.
Providing relevant knowledge can assist LLMs in identifying hallucinated responses.
The transition between hidden states encodes truthfulness information.
papers.limitation:
Do not differentiate between fine-grained categories of hallucination.
Do not examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers, only the final layer.
Experiments are performed on conventional QA tasks, not more complicated or domain-specific tasks.
Future research is needed to develop more effective strategies for mitigating LLM hallucination.
future_direction: Explore different types of hallucination (factual fabrication, instruction inconsistency, etc.).
Examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers and investigate layer-by-layer formation of hallucination.
Adapt the experimental framework to more complicated or domain-specific tasks and potentially extend to multimodal features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make up answers that are not real, and this is known as hallucination. This research aims to see if, how, and to what extent LLMs are aware of hallucination. More specifically, we check whether and how an LLM reacts differently in its hidden states when it answers a question right versus when it hallucinates. To do this, we introduce an experimental framework which allows examining LLM's hidden states in different hallucination situations. Building upon this framework, we conduct a series of experiments with language models in the LLaMA family (Touvron et al., 2023). Our empirical findings suggest that LLMs react differently when processing a genuine response versus a fabricated one. We then apply various model interpretation techniques to help understand and explain the findings better. Moreover, informed by the empirical observations, we show great potential of using the guidance derived from LLM's hidden representation space to mitigate hallucination. We believe this work provides insights into how LLMs produce hallucinated answers and how to make them occur less often.

papers.title: Multi-Neuron Representations of Hierarchical Concepts in Spiking Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can hierarchical concepts be represented in spiking neural networks to support fault-tolerant recognition when partial information is presented and neurons may fail?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces multi-neuron representations of hierarchical concepts in spiking neural networks for fault-tolerant recognition under partial information and neuron failures, with probabilistic analysis of recognition success.
papers.conclusion: Multi-neuron representations enable fault-tolerant recognition of hierarchical concepts in spiking neural networks under partial information and neuron failures, with analysis providing probabilistic guarantees.
papers.key_findings:
Recognition works correctly in three types of spiking neural networks with high probability, depending on the number of representative neurons and the neuron failure probability.
The probability of correct recognition increases with the number of representatives and decreases with the failure probability.
Representations using multiple neurons per concept provide redundancy and fault tolerance.
Learning algorithms for these representations are discussed, inspired by prior work on Hebbian learning and assembly calculus.
papers.limitation:
Strong uniformity assumptions, such as all concepts having the same number of children and neurons failing independently with the same probability.
The analysis may not yield the tightest possible bounds.
The model omits feedback edges and considers only initial random failures.
future_direction: Simulating the algorithms to evaluate performance and improve analysis.
Extending the failure model to include online failures.
Incorporating feedback edges into the network model.
Completing the analysis of the proposed learning algorithms, especially for networks with lateral edges.
papers.abstract: We describe how hierarchical concepts can be represented in three types of layered neural networks. The aim is to support recognition of the concepts when partial information about the concepts is presented, and also when some of the neurons in the network might fail. Our failure model involves initial random failures. The three types of networks are: feed-forward networks with high connectivity, feed-forward networks with low connectivity, and layered networks with low connectivity and with both forward edges and "lateral" edges within layers. In order to achieve fault-tolerance, the representations all use multiple representative neurons for each concept. We show how recognition can work in all three of these settings, and quantify how the probability of correct recognition depends on several parameters, including the number of representatives and the neuron failure probability. We also discuss how these representations might be learned, in all three types of networks. For the feed-forward networks, the learning algorithms are similar to ones used in [4], whereas for networks with lateral edges, the algorithms are generally inspired by work on the assembly calculus [3, 6, 7].

papers.title: Revealing emergent human-like conceptual representations from language prediction
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) develop human-like concepts through language prediction, and how such concepts are represented, organized, and linked to behavior.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that structured, human-like conceptual representations can emerge in LLMs purely from language prediction, without real-world grounding. These representations converge to a shared, context-independent structure that predicts model performance and aligns with human behavioral and neural data.
papers.conclusion: The findings establish that critical aspects of human conceptual representation and organization can emerge purely from language prediction in LLMs, offering a tractable window into human concepts and advancing alignment between artificial and human intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can flexibly derive concepts from definitional descriptions using in-context learning, with performance improving with more demonstrations.
The conceptual representations formed by LLMs converge toward a shared, context-independent relational structure as the number of contextual demonstrations increases.
Alignment of a model's conceptual representations with this convergent structure reliably predicts its performance on a range of language understanding and reasoning tasks.
LLM-derived conceptual representations effectively predict human behavioral judgments, such as similarity ratings and categorization, outperforming static word embeddings.
The convergent conceptual representations align closely with neural activity patterns in the human brain, providing evidence for their biological plausibility.
papers.limitation: LLMs struggled to predict human judgments when they relied on perceptual properties like color or texture, indicating a divergence from human judgments in visually grounded dimensions.
papers.abstract: People acquire concepts through rich physical and social experiences and use them to understand and navigate the world. In contrast, large language models (LLMs), trained solely through next-token prediction on text, exhibit strikingly human-like behaviors. Are these models developing concepts akin to those of humans? If so, how are such concepts represented, organized, and related to behavior? Here, we address these questions by investigating the representations formed by LLMs during an in-context concept inference task. We found that LLMs can flexibly derive concepts from linguistic descriptions in relation to contextual cues about other concepts. The derived representations converge toward a shared, context-independent structure, and alignment with this structure reliably predicts model performance across various understanding and reasoning tasks. Moreover, the convergent representations effectively capture human behavioral judgments and closely align with neural activity patterns in the human brain, providing evidence for biological plausibility. Together, these findings establish that structured, human-like conceptual representations can emerge purely from language prediction without real-world grounding, highlighting the role of conceptual structure in understanding intelligent behavior. More broadly, our work suggests that LLMs offer a tangible window into the nature of human concepts and lays the groundwork for advancing alignment between artificial and human intelligence.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: The Evolution of Representation in Simple Cognitive Networks
papers.research_question: How are representations developed in cognitive systems, and are they necessary for intelligent behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an information-theoretic measure of representation (R) and shows that the capacity to represent increases during evolutionary adaptation in simple cognitive networks.
papers.conclusion: The measure R can quantify representations in any cognitive system and should be predictive of an agent's long-term adaptive success.
papers.key_findings:
The representation measure R increases during evolutionary adaptation in both artificial neural networks and Markov brains.
Markov brains evolve to become less dependent on sensory inputs and more dependent on internal states than artificial neural networks.
Networks form representations of specific environmental features (concepts) and these representations are distributed across nodes.
Representations are formed over the lifetime of the agent, building up as the agent integrates information.
The evolved networks can be analyzed to determine which nodes represent which environmental features.
future_direction: Future investigations on what kind of system is more powerful for making intelligent decisions using representations.
papers.abstract: Representations are internal models of the environment that can provide guidance to a behaving agent, even in the absence of sensory information. It is not clear how representations are developed and whether they are necessary or even essential for intelligent behavior. We argue here that the ability to represent relevant features of the environment is the expected consequence of an adaptive process, give a formal definition of representation based on information theory, and quantify it with a measure R. To measure how R changes over time, we evolve two types of networks--an artificial neural network and a network of hidden Markov gates--to solve a categorization task using a genetic algorithm. We find that the capacity to represent increases during evolutionary adaptation and that agents form representations of their environment during their lifetime. This ability allows the agents to act on sensorial inputs in the context of their acquired representations and enables complex and context-dependent behavior. We examine which concepts (features of the environment) our networks are representing, how the representations are logically encoded in the networks, and how they form as an agent behaves to solve a task. We conclude that R should be able to quantify the representations within any cognitive system and should be predictive of an agent's long-term adaptive success.

papers.title: Bilinear relational structure fixes reversal curse and enables consistent model editing
papers.research_question: Is the reversal curse an inherent limitation of language models, and can it be mitigated by learning a bilinear relational structure in internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The reversal curse and model editing failures are not inherent but stem from unstructured knowledge representations; training with appropriate regularization induces a bilinear relational structure that mitigates the curse and enables logically consistent editing.
papers.conclusion: The reversal curse and editing generalization failures are symptoms of unstructured internal knowledge representations; inducing bilinear relational geometry through training and regularization leads to more reliable and editable language models.
papers.key_findings:
Weight decay regularization enables models to overcome the reversal curse by learning a more generalizable internal structure.
Successful models develop a robust bilinear relational structure in their hidden representations, peaking in middle layers.
The learned bilinear matrices obey algebraic properties (inversion via transpose, composition via product), enabling multi-hop inference.
Models with bilinear structure successfully propagate single-fact edits to logically entailed facts (reverse and neighborhood relations).
A strong positive correlation exists between a model's bilinear probe accuracy and its logical generalization performance after editing.
papers.limitation: The study uses language models trained from scratch on a clean, synthetic dataset, which may not scale to large, pre-trained language models with noisy, complex knowledge.
future_direction: Investigate whether similar bilinear structures exist in large-scale pre-trained language models.
Develop geometry-aware editing algorithms that leverage internal relational structures.
Explore 'architectural preparation' strategies to endow models with structured knowledge representations during pre-training or fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The reversal curse -- a language model's (LM) inability to infer an unseen fact ``B is A'' from a learned fact ``A is B'' -- is widely considered a fundamental limitation. We show that this is not an inherent failure but an artifact of how models encode knowledge. By training LMs from scratch on a synthetic dataset of relational knowledge graphs, we demonstrate that bilinear relational structure emerges in their hidden representations. This structure substantially alleviates the reversal curse, enabling LMs to infer unseen reverse facts. Crucially, we also find that this bilinear structure plays a key role in consistent model editing. When a fact is updated in a LM with this structure, the edit correctly propagates to its reverse and other logically dependent facts. In contrast, models lacking this representation not only suffer from the reversal curse but also fail to generalize edits, further introducing logical inconsistencies. Our results establish that training on a relational knowledge dataset induces the emergence of bilinear internal representations, which in turn enable LMs to behave in a logically consistent manner after editing. This implies that the success of model editing depends critically not just on editing algorithms but on the underlying representational geometry of the knowledge being modified.

papers.title: Analysing the Residual Stream of Language Models Under Knowledge Conflicts
papers.research_question: Can we identify the conflict between context and parameter knowledge by probing the residual stream? Can we know which source of knowledge the models will use before they generate the answers?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally register knowledge conflict signals in the residual stream, which can be detected by probing intermediate activations. The residual stream shows distinct skewness patterns when the model relies on contextual versus parametric knowledge, enabling prediction of the model's knowledge selection behavior.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit internal mechanisms for identifying conflicts in the mid-layers, and the residual stream shows distinct skewness patterns when the model uses context and parametric knowledge to predict. This analysis provides insights into the behaviour of LLMs in the presence of knowledge conflicts.
papers.key_findings:
The signal of knowledge conflict rises from intermediate layers (e.g., layer 13-14) and can be detected with high accuracy using linear probing.
The residual stream exhibits different skewness patterns (measured by Kurtosis, Hoyer, Gini) when the model uses contextual knowledge versus parametric knowledge.
The decision of which knowledge to use occurs after the detection of the knowledge conflict signal.
The probing model's performance for conflict detection peaks around the 14th layer and then decreases slightly.
The skewness patterns are more pronounced in hidden states than in MLP or Self-Attention activations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a significant amount of factual knowledge in their parameters. However, their parametric knowledge may conflict with the information provided in the context. Such conflicts can lead to undesirable model behaviour, such as reliance on outdated or incorrect information. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can identify knowledge conflicts and whether it is possible to know which source of knowledge the model will rely on by analysing the residual stream of the LLM. Through probing tasks, we find that LLMs can internally register the signal of knowledge conflict in the residual stream, which can be accurately detected by probing the intermediate model activations. This allows us to detect conflicts within the residual stream before generating the answers without modifying the input or model parameters. Moreover, we find that the residual stream shows significantly different patterns when the model relies on contextual knowledge versus parametric knowledge to resolve conflicts. This pattern can be employed to estimate the behaviour of LLMs when conflict happens and prevent unexpected answers before producing the answers. Our analysis offers insights into how LLMs internally manage knowledge conflicts and provides a foundation for developing methods to control the knowledge selection processes.

papers.title: Trees in transformers: a theoretical analysis of the Transformer's ability to represent trees
papers.research_question: Can Transformer networks capture tree structures, what are the limits of this ability, and how can the learning process be made more efficient?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves theoretically that a 1-layer Transformer can find tree backbone vectors and that two linear layers with ReLU can recover any tree backbone from two linearly independent starting backbones, and empirically shows standard Transformers can learn tree structures, albeit with slower convergence than when tree position is explicitly encoded.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can capture tree structures; a 1-layer 1-head Transformer can handle trees within its input length limit, but a 2-layer Transformer is necessary to learn all possible tree backbones, and learning efficiency can be improved by explicitly encoding tree structure information.
papers.key_findings:
A 1-layer, 1 attention head Transformer can find the backbone vector for any tree (Proposition 1).
Two linear layers with ReLU activation can recover any tree backbone from any two nonzero, linearly independent starting backbones (Theorem 1).
Standard Transformers achieve similar accuracy compared to Transformers with explicit tree position encoding, but with slower convergence.
Transformers can learn tree structures in practice, as shown by synthetic experiments.
Explicit tree positional encodings lead to faster convergence and sometimes higher accuracy in tree transduction tasks.
papers.limitation: Experiments are conducted on synthetic data, so generalization to real-world data is unclear.
future_direction: Further (computationally intensive) experiments to understand the asymptotic boundary of how much tree information benefits training.
Investigating deeper networks or more training steps for hard tasks like parent12 and parent123.
papers.abstract: Transformer networks are the de facto standard architecture in natural language processing. To date, there are no theoretical analyses of the Transformer's ability to capture tree structures. We focus on the ability of Transformer networks to learn tree structures that are important for tree transduction problems. We first analyze the theoretical capability of the standard Transformer architecture to learn tree structures given enumeration of all possible tree backbones, which we define as trees without labels. We then prove that two linear layers with ReLU activation function can recover any tree backbone from any two nonzero, linearly independent starting backbones. This implies that a Transformer can learn tree structures well in theory. We conduct experiments with synthetic data and find that the standard Transformer achieves similar accuracy compared to a Transformer where tree position information is explicitly encoded, albeit with slower convergence. This confirms empirically that Transformers can learn tree structures.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: BERTnesia: Investigating the capture and forgetting of knowledge in BERT
papers.research_question: How is relational knowledge distributed across BERT's layers, and how does fine-tuning affect the retention and forgetting of such knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a layerwise probing framework for BERT and finds that intermediate layers contain significant relational knowledge, which is forgotten during fine-tuning, with the extent of forgetting depending on the fine-tuning objective.
papers.conclusion: The proposed layerwise probing framework reveals that BERT stores significant knowledge in intermediate layers, which is forgotten during fine-tuning, with ranking tasks mitigating forgetting more than QA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers contain a substantial amount of knowledge (17-60% of total knowledge) that is not present in the last layer.
Relational knowledge emerges at varying rates across layers, with some relation types doubling in the last layer and others being maximally captured in intermediate layers.
Fine-tuning causes forgetting of relational knowledge, but the amount of forgetting is influenced by the fine-tuning objective, not the dataset size.
Ranking models forget the least and retain more knowledge in their final layer compared to QA models.
The total knowledge in BERT is underestimated when only the last layer is probed.
papers.limitation:
Probing with cloze statements may conflate task-specific knowledge (masked word prediction) with factual knowledge, especially for MLM models.
Probes are limited to single-token factual knowledge, excluding multi-word entities and relations.
future_direction: Investigating ranking models with different training objectives (pointwise, pairwise, listwise).
Studying knowledge-intensive QA models like answer generation models.
Applying the framework to study variants of BERT architecture and pre-training methods.
papers.abstract: Probing complex language models has recently revealed several insights into linguistic and semantic patterns found in the learned representations. In this paper, we probe BERT specifically to understand and measure the relational knowledge it captures. We utilize knowledge base completion tasks to probe every layer of pre-trained as well as fine-tuned BERT (ranking, question answering, NER). Our findings show that knowledge is not just contained in BERT's final layers. Intermediate layers contribute a significant amount (17-60%) to the total knowledge found. Probing intermediate layers also reveals how different types of knowledge emerge at varying rates. When BERT is fine-tuned, relational knowledge is forgotten but the extent of forgetting is impacted by the fine-tuning objective but not the size of the dataset. We found that ranking models forget the least and retain more knowledge in their final layer. We release our code on github 1 to repeat the experiments.

papers.title: Inspecting the concept knowledge graph encoded by modern language models
papers.research_question: To what extent do pre-trained language models encode semantic information, specifically the concept relations embedded in WordNet?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-trained language models encode relevant knowledge about WordNet concept relations but with imprecisions, and different model families exhibit different biases in how and where they encode this semantic information.
papers.conclusion: Pre-trained language models learn relevant knowledge about the organization of concepts in WordNet but contain several imprecisions, and different model families exhibit dissimilar behaviors due to different biases.
papers.key_findings:
All models encode a relevant amount of knowledge about semantic relations in WordNet, but this knowledge contains imprecisions.
The ability to learn concept relations depends on how frequent and specific the concepts are, with non-contextualized and generative models more affected by frequency.
Some semantic categories, such as 'taxonomic groups', are challenging for all models, while others are family-specific.
Contextualized models are unaffected by multi-sense words, suggesting they rely heavily on context.
Models encode semantic knowledge in different layers depending on architecture; for example, BERT and RoBERTa use top layers, while XLNet and ALBERT use first layers.
future_direction: Combining model families as ensembles to leverage their different strengths.
Using adaptive strategies (e.g., early exiting) that exploit layers where semantic knowledge is encoded.
Training larger models without increasing corpus size to improve semantic capabilities.
papers.abstract: The field of natural language understanding has experienced exponential progress in the last few years, with impressive results in several tasks. This success has motivated researchers to study the underlying knowledge encoded by these models. Despite this, attempts to understand their semantic capabilities have not been successful, often leading to non-conclusive, or contradictory conclusions among different works. Via a probing classifier, we extract the underlying knowledge graph of nine of the most influential language models of the last years, including word embeddings, text generators, and context encoders. This probe is based on concept relatedness, grounded on WordNet. Our results reveal that all the models encode this knowledge, but suffer from several inaccuracies. Furthermore, we show that the different architectures and training strategies lead to different model biases. We conduct a systematic evaluation to discover specific factors that explain why some concepts are challenging. We hope our insights will motivate the development of models that capture concepts more precisely.

papers.title: Truth is Universal: Robust Detection of Lies in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we robustly detect when Large Language Models (LLMs) are lying by analyzing their internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a universal two-dimensional subspace in LLM activations containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP), which explains prior generalization failures and enables the construction of a robust lie detector (TTPD).
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates a universal two-dimensional internal representation of truth in LLMs, clarifies prior generalization failures, and provides a robust method (TTPD) for lie detection, advancing towards general-purpose, transparent, and safe AI.
papers.key_findings:
A two-dimensional subspace in the residual stream activations separates true and false statements, containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP).
The affirmative truth direction (tA) from prior work is a linear combination of tG and tP, explaining its failure to generalize to negated statements.
The two-dimensional truth representation is universal across multiple LLM families and sizes (e.g., LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral).
The proposed TTPD method, which uses the tG direction, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (94%) in detecting lies in both simple factual statements and complex real-world scenarios.
The truth subspace remains two-dimensional even when considering more complex statement types (logical conjunctions/disjunctions) and different languages (German).
papers.limitation:
TTPD uses only one of the two dimensions (tG) of the truth subspace; a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP might achieve higher accuracy.
The generalization of TTPD is tested on a limited number of statement types and real-world scenarios.
The analysis only shows the truth subspace is at least two-dimensional; examining more statement types might reveal additional linear or non-linear structures.
The findings' applicability to larger LLMs or multimodal models is not tested.
future_direction: Explore a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP for higher accuracy.
Test generalization across a broader range of statement types and diverse real-world contexts.
Study the effects of interventions on the 2D truth subspace during inference on model outputs.
Determine whether the findings apply to larger LLMs or multimodal models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionised natural language processing, exhibiting impressive human-like capabilities. In particular, LLMs are capable of "lying", knowingly outputting false statements. Hence, it is of interest and importance to develop methods to detect when LLMs lie. Indeed, several authors trained classifiers to detect LLM lies based on their internal model activations. However, other researchers showed that these classifiers may fail to generalise, for example to negated statements. In this work, we aim to develop a robust method to detect when an LLM is lying. To this end, we make the following key contributions: (i) We demonstrate the existence of a two-dimensional subspace, along which the activation vectors of true and false statements can be separated. Notably, this finding is universal and holds for various LLMs, including Gemma-7B, LLaMA2-13B, Mistral-7B and LLaMA3-8B. Our analysis explains the generalisation failures observed in previous studies and sets the stage for more robust lie detection; (ii) Building upon (i), we construct an accurate LLM lie detector. Empirically, our proposed classifier achieves state-of-the-art performance, attaining 94% accuracy in both distinguishing true from false factual statements and detecting lies generated in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Grounding LLM Reasoning with Knowledge Graphs
papers.research_question: How can grounding LLM reasoning in knowledge graphs improve accuracy and interpretability by linking each reasoning step to structured graph data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that grounds LLM reasoning in knowledge graphs by linking each reasoning step to graph data, improving both accuracy and interpretability on complex question-answering tasks.
papers.conclusion: Grounding LLM reasoning in knowledge graphs by integrating reasoning steps with structured retrieval improves accuracy and offers a more interpretable view of the reasoning process, suggesting a path toward systematic and transparent reasoning interventions.
papers.key_findings:
The agentic method for graph interaction generally outperforms automatic graph exploration, indicating targeted interventions enhance accuracy.
The Tree-of-Thought (ToT) reasoning strategy shows superior performance by exploring multiple reasoning paths.
Graph-of-Thought (GoT) does not outperform ToT, revealing challenges in merging divergent reasoning paths effectively.
Performance improves with more reasoning steps for agentic methods, while automatic exploration performs well with fewer steps.
The framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on GRBench, with at least 26.5% improvement over Chain-of-Thought baselines.
papers.limitation:
Computational complexity grows exponentially for Tree-of-Thought and Graph-of-Thought due to branching, limiting scalability.
Effectiveness depends on the coverage and quality of the underlying knowledge graph.
LLMs may still hallucinate despite grounding in graph structure.
future_direction: Extending the framework to larger and more heterogeneous graphs.
Exploring how structured retrieval can guide reasoning in domains where accuracy and verifiability are critical.
Developing more advanced intervention strategies for merging partial reasoning outcomes.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at generating natural language answers, yet their outputs often remain unverifiable and difficult to trace. Knowledge Graphs (KGs) offer a complementary strength by representing entities and their relationships in structured form, providing a foundation for more reliable reasoning. We propose a novel framework that integrates LLM reasoning with KGs by linking each step of the reasoning process to graph-structured data. This grounding turns intermediate ``thoughts'' into interpretable traces that remain consistent with external knowledge. Our approach incorporates multiple reasoning strategies, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Tree-of-Thought (ToT), and Graph-of-Thought (GoT), and is evaluated on GRBench, a benchmark for domain-specific graph reasoning. Our experiments show state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance, with at least 26.5\% improvement over CoT baselines. Beyond accuracy, we analyze how step depth, branching structure, and model size influence reasoning quality, offering insights into the conditions that support effective reasoning. Together, these contributions highlight how grounding LLMs in structured knowledge enables both higher accuracy and greater interpretability in complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Probing the Representational Structure of Regular Polysemy via Sense Analogy Questions: Insights from Contextual Word Vectors
papers.research_question: How does the BERT model represent regular polysemy? Specifically, does it reflect shared structure within regular relationships, variation in regularity across relationships, higher-order latent structure shared across relationships, and is this explained by meaning overlap?
papers.core_contribution: The LRcos model demonstrates that BERT's contextual embeddings capture the shared representational structure of regular polysemy, showing sensitivity to within-relationship regularity, variation across relationships (a 'regularity continuum'), shared higher-order latent structure, and that these effects are not fully explained by meaning overlap.
papers.conclusion: The findings enrich theoretical work on regular polysemy with a computationally explicit method and provide evidence for an organizational principle in the mental lexicon and conceptual knowledge system.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's embeddings are sensitive to the shared structure within a given regular polysemy relationship.
The degree of regularity varies across different regular relationships, suggesting a 'regularity continuum'.
There is higher-order latent structure shared across different regular relationships.
The effects are not explained by meaning overlap between senses.
Both components of the LRcos model (logistic regression and cosine similarity) contribute to accurate sense analogy answering.
papers.abstract: Regular polysemes are sets of ambiguous words that all share the same relationship between their meanings, such as CHICKEN and LOBSTER both referring to an animal or its meat. To probe how a distributional semantic model, here exemplified by bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT), represents regular polysemy, we analyzed whether its embeddings support answering sense analogy questions similar to "is the mapping between CHICKEN (as an animal) and CHICKEN (as a meat) similar to that which maps between LOBSTER (as an animal) to LOBSTER (as a meat)?" We did so using the LRcos model, which combines a logistic regression classifier of different categories (e.g., animal vs. meat) with a measure of cosine similarity. We found that (a) the model was sensitive to the shared structure within a given regular relationship; (b) the shared structure varies across different regular relationships (e.g., animal/meat vs. location/organization), potentially reflective of a "regularity continuum;" (c) some high-order latent structure is shared across different regular relationships, suggestive of a similar latent structure across different types of relationships; and (d) there is a lack of evidence for the aforementioned effects being explained by meaning overlap. Lastly, we found that both components of the LRcos model made important contributions to accurate responding and that a variation of this method could yield an accuracy boost of 10% in answering sense analogy questions. These findings enrich previous theoretical work on regular polysemy with a computationally explicit theory and methods, and provide evidence for an important organizational principle for the mental lexicon and the broader conceptual knowledge system.

papers.title: Cross-model Transferability among Large Language Models on the Platonic Representations of Concepts
papers.research_question: How can conceptual representations (steering vectors) be transferred across different large language models to enable cross-model behavioral control?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces L-Cross Modulation, a linear transformation method to transfer steering vectors across LLMs, demonstrating that conceptual representations are linearly alignable and transferable, even from weaker to stronger models.
papers.conclusion: Cross-model transferability of conceptual representations is achievable via linear transformations, revealing a fundamental universality in how LLMs encode concepts, paving the way for more universal and adaptable language models.
papers.key_findings:
L-Cross Modulation effectively modulates target LLMs using steering vectors transferred from source LLMs.
The linear transformation matrix generalizes across different concepts, enabling alignment of SVs for multiple concepts.
Weak-to-strong transferability: SVs extracted from smaller LLMs can effectively modulate the behavior of larger LLMs.
papers.limitation:
The scope of concepts is limited to eleven benchmark concepts; creating more datasets is resource-intensive.
The evaluation metrics are diverse and may not generalize fully to all concepts.
The hyper-parameter (β) for applying steering vectors is manually tuned rather than automatically optimized.
future_direction: Expand to more high-level concepts with additional datasets.
Develop a unified, comprehensive evaluation framework including a standardized dataset and benchmark.
Automatically determine optimal hyperparameters for applying steering vectors.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical research frontier. Prior research has shown that a single LLM's concept representations can be captured as steering vectors (SVs), enabling the control of LLM behavior (e.g., towards generating harmful content). Our work takes a novel approach by exploring the intricate relationships between concept representations across different LLMs, drawing an intriguing parallel to Plato's Allegory of the Cave. In particular, we introduce a linear transformation method to bridge these representations and present three key findings: 1) Concept representations across different LLMs can be effectively aligned using simple linear transformations, enabling efficient cross-model transfer and behavioral control via SVs. 2) This linear transformation generalizes across concepts, facilitating alignment and control of SVs representing different concepts across LLMs. 3) A weak-to-strong transferability exists between LLM concept representations, whereby SVs extracted from smaller LLMs can effectively control the behavior of larger LLMs.

papers.title: Associative memory inspires improvements for in-context learning using a novel attention residual stream architecture
papers.research_question: How can insights from associative memory models be used to improve in-context learning (ICL) in Transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory, that allows information to flow directly between attention heads, leading to faster and improved in-context learning in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: The residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory models, improves in-context learning in Transformers and shows promising scalability to larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
A one-layer associative memory model (AMICL) can perform in-context learning on a classification task.
Adding a residual stream for attention values (and to a lesser extent, queries) in a two-layer Transformer speeds up the emergence of ICL during training compared to a classic Transformer.
Naively applying the residual value stream architecture to small language models (8M and 1B parameters) trained on Tiny Stories indicates performance improvements scale to larger models and more naturalistic data.
future_direction: Testing the residual attention stream architecture on larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the interpretability of the residual stream for understanding model mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive ability to utilise information within the context of their input sequences to appropriately respond to data unseen by the LLM during its training procedure. This ability is known as in-context learning (ICL). Humans and non-human animals demonstrate similar abilities, however their neural architectures differ substantially from LLMs. Despite this, a critical component within LLMs, the attention mechanism, resembles modern associative memory models, widely used in and influenced by the computational neuroscience community to model biological memory systems. Using this connection, we introduce an associative memory model capable of performing ICL. We use this as inspiration for a novel residual stream architecture which allows information to directly flow between attention heads. We test this architecture during training within a two-layer Transformer and show its ICL abilities manifest more quickly than without this modification. We then apply our architecture in small language models with 8 million and 1 billion parameters, focusing on attention head values, with results also indicating improved performance at these larger and more naturalistic scales.

papers.title: Behavioural vs. Representational Systematicity in End-to-End Models: An Opinionated Survey
papers.research_question: What is the distinction between behavioural and representational systematicity in ML models, and to what extent do existing benchmarks test for these different types of systematicity?
papers.core_contribution: This paper disentangles behavioural and representational systematicity, arguing that many existing benchmarks focus on the former while Fodor and Pylyshyn's challenge concerns the latter. It analyzes key benchmarks using Hadley's taxonomy and highlights the need for mechanistic interpretability to assess representational systematicity.
papers.conclusion: Meaningful progress toward human-like systematic generalization requires appropriately-scoped behavioural claims backed by rigorous mechanistic interpretability to assess the systematicity of internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Many existing benchmarks for systematic generalization (e.g., SCAN, PCFG SET) primarily test weak or quasi-systematicity, not the strong systematicity closest to human generalization.
The conflation of behavioural and representational systematicity has led to misunderstandings about the systematic generalization capabilities of neural networks.
Mechanistic interpretability is crucial for validating operationalizations of systematicity and for drawing conclusions about a model's internal representations from its behaviour.
In vision, the lack of a clear theory of compositionality makes it difficult to define and test for systematicity analogous to linguistic systematicity.
papers.abstract: A core aspect of compositionality, systematicity is a desirable property in ML models as it enables strong generalization to novel contexts. This has led to numerous studies proposing benchmarks to assess systematic generalization, as well as models and training regimes designed to enhance it. Many of these efforts are framed as addressing the challenge posed by Fodor and Pylyshyn. However, while they argue for systematicity of representations, existing benchmarks and models primarily focus on the systematicity of behaviour. We emphasize the crucial nature of this distinction. Furthermore, building on Hadley's (1994) taxonomy of systematic generalization, we analyze the extent to which behavioural systematicity is tested by key benchmarks in the literature across language and vision. Finally, we highlight ways of assessing systematicity of representations in ML models as practiced in the field of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Contextual Feature Extraction Hierarchies Converge in Large Language Models and the Brain
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to the alignment of large language models (LLMs) with the brain's language processing mechanisms, and do LLMs share fundamental computational principles that increasingly align with the spoken language processing pathway in the human brain?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that higher-performing large language models (LLMs) exhibit greater alignment with the brain's hierarchical language processing, and that contextual information is a key factor driving this convergence.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that hierarchical structure and contextual dependencies are fundamental to language processing, leading to convergent strategies in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Higher-performing LLMs achieve higher peak brain similarity scores.
Better-performing LLMs peak in brain similarity at earlier layers compared to lower-performing models.
Better-performing LLMs have hierarchical feature extraction pathways that more closely align with the brain's hierarchy.
Contextual information is crucial for brain similarity and hierarchy alignment, with long context windows being particularly important.
Top-performing LLMs converge in their feature extraction hierarchies, as shown by high inter-model similarity.
papers.limitation:
Limited iEEG coverage may not capture all relevant brain regions.
The speech comprehension task is simple and may not fully engage higher-level language processing.
LLMs are trained for next-word prediction, which differs from the comprehension task performed by subjects.
future_direction: Using brain similarity as an evaluation metric for LLM development.
Improving contextual processing in LLMs to enhance performance and brain alignment.
Investigating the role of later layers in LLMs for higher-order integration.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have sparked interest in the parallels between large language models (LLMs) and human neural processing, particularly in language comprehension. While prior research has established similarities in the representation of LLMs and the brain, the underlying computational principles that cause this convergence, especially in the context of evolving LLMs, remain elusive. Here, we examined a diverse selection of high-performance LLMs with similar parameter sizes to investigate the factors contributing to their alignment with the brain's language processing mechanisms. We find that as LLMs achieve higher performance on benchmark tasks, they not only become more brain-like as measured by higher performance when predicting neural responses from LLM embeddings, but also their hierarchical feature extraction pathways map more closely onto the brain's while using fewer layers to do the same encoding. We also compare the feature extraction pathways of the LLMs to each other and identify new ways in which high-performing models have converged toward similar hierarchical processing mechanisms. Finally, we show the importance of contextual information in improving model performance and brain similarity. Our findings reveal the converging aspects of language processing in the brain and LLMs and offer new directions for developing models that align more closely with human cognitive processing.

papers.title: Revealing the Deceptiveness of Knowledge Editing: A Mechanistic Analysis of Superficial Editing
papers.research_question: Why do knowledge-edited language models revert to their original knowledge when presented with carefully crafted prompts (attack probes), despite appearing successfully edited according to conventional metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of superficial editing, provides evaluation datasets and metrics, and identifies two key mechanistic factors: the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and specific attention modules in later layers, showing that specific attention heads and their left singular vectors encode original knowledge and cause superficial editing.
papers.conclusion: Superficial editing is a significant challenge for knowledge editing, and the mechanistic analysis reveals the underlying factors in the residual stream and attention modules, with broader applicability to unlearning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect conventional metrics but are vulnerable to attack probes, exhibiting superficial editing in over 70% of cases for some methods.
The residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers shows inhibited enrichment of new knowledge and limited accumulation of original knowledge.
Later attention modules cause the Reversal of the Residual Stream (RRS) phenomenon by incorporating original knowledge into the last position, leading to superficial editing.
Specific attention heads in later layers and their left singular vectors are causally responsible for encoding original knowledge and inducing superficial editing.
Similar patterns are observed in superficial unlearning, demonstrating the generality of the findings.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing, which aims to update the knowledge encoded in language models, can be deceptive. Despite the fact that many existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect performance on conventional metrics, the models edited by them are still prone to generating original knowledge. This paper introduces the concept of "superficial editing" to describe this phenomenon. Our comprehensive evaluation reveals that this issue presents a significant challenge to existing algorithms. Through systematic investigation, we identify and validate two key factors contributing to this issue: (1) the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and (2) specific attention modules in later layers. Notably, certain attention heads in later layers, along with specific left singular vectors in their output matrices, encapsulate the original knowledge and exhibit a causal relationship with superficial editing. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to the task of superficial unlearning, where we observe consistent patterns in the behavior of specific attention heads and their corresponding left singular vectors, thereby demonstrating the robustness and broader applicability of our methodology and conclusions. Our code is available here.

papers.title: Representation in large language models
papers.research_question: Is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, contrary to the look-up table view, and outlines how mechanistic interpretability methods can be used to study these representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do use representation-based information processing, and we can investigate these representations using mechanistic interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
The look-up table view of LLMs is inadequate because it cannot explain robust behavior.
Representations, as defined by four conditions (INFORMATION, EXPLOITABILITY, BEHAVIOR, ROLE), can explain robust behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability methods like probing and causal interventions can test for representations in LLMs.
papers.abstract: The extraordinary success of recent Large Language Models (LLMs) on a diverse array of tasks has led to an explosion of scientific and philosophical theorizing aimed at explaining how they do what they do. Unfortunately, disagreement over fundamental theoretical issues has led to stalemate, with entrenched camps of LLM optimists and pessimists often committed to very different views of how these systems work. Overcoming stalemate requires agreement on fundamental questions, and the goal of this paper is to address one such question, namely: is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up? This is a question about what kind of algorithm LLMs implement, and the answer carries serious implications for higher level questions about whether these systems have beliefs, intentions, concepts, knowledge, and understanding. I argue that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, and then I describe and defend a series of practical techniques for investigating these representations and developing explanations on their basis. The resulting account provides a groundwork for future theorizing about language models and their successors.

papers.title: Towards Mechanistic Interpretability of Graph Transformers via Attention Graphs
papers.research_question: When Graph Transformers are allowed to learn the optimal graph structure using all-to-all attention among input nodes, do the learned Attention Graphs correlate with the input graph structure? And for heterophilous graphs, can different Graph Transformer variants achieve similar performance while utilising distinct information flow patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Attention Graphs, a framework for mechanistic interpretability of Graph Neural Networks and Graph Transformers, and finds that learned attention patterns do not necessarily recover the input graph structure and that different architectures can implement distinct algorithmic strategies despite similar performance.
papers.conclusion: Attention Graphs provide a framework for mechanistic interpretability of GNNs and Graph Transformers, revealing that different inductive biases lead to distinct algorithmic strategies despite similar performance, challenging evaluation solely based on accuracy metrics.
papers.key_findings:
When Graph Transformers learn with all-to-all attention, the learned Attention Graphs do not tend to correlate with the input graph structure.
For heterophilous graphs, different Graph Transformer variants achieve similar performance while utilising distinct information flow patterns.
Certain nodes emerge as pivotal, disproportionately influencing predictions across the graph regardless of topological distance.
DLB models exhibit strong self-attention patterns (diagonals), suggesting focus on initial node features, while DL models develop reference nodes (verticals) that receive high attention from all other nodes.
The Attention Graph framework enables network science analysis of information flow in Graph Transformers.
papers.limitation:
Matrix multiplication may not capture non-linear interactions from activation functions between layers.
Aggregating heterogeneous attention patterns across heads and layers into a single matrix may oversimplify complex model dynamics.
Experiments are limited to small models (up to 2 layers, 2 heads) and node classification tasks.
future_direction: Extend the Attention Graph framework to more complex graph architectures and inductive tasks.
Apply network science and graph theory tools like spectral analysis, community detection, and information flow dynamics to analyze Transformers.
papers.abstract: We introduce Attention Graphs, a new tool for mechanistic interpretability of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Graph Transformers based on the mathematical equivalence between message passing in GNNs and the self-attention mechanism in Transformers. Attention Graphs aggregate attention matrices across Transformer layers and heads to describe how information flows among input nodes. Through experiments on homophilous and heterophilous node classification tasks, we analyze Attention Graphs from a network science perspective and find that: (1) When Graph Transformers are allowed to learn the optimal graph structure using all-to-all attention among input nodes, the Attention Graphs learned by the model do not tend to correlate with the input/original graph structure; and (2) For heterophilous graphs, different Graph Transformer variants can achieve similar performance while utilising distinct information flow patterns. Open source code: https://github.com/batu-el/understanding-inductive-biases-of-gnns

papers.title: From Chains to DAGs: Probing the Graph Structure of Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the internal representation of LLMs encode graph-structured reasoning (as directed acyclic graphs) beyond linear chains, and where does this structure emerge across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Reasoning DAG Probing, a framework to test whether LLM hidden states linearly encode reasoning DAG structure, and finds that such structure is meaningfully encoded, peaking in intermediate layers, and varies with node depth, edge span, and model scale.
papers.conclusion: LLM reasoning is not purely sequential, but exhibits measurable internal graph structure.
papers.key_findings:
DAG structure is meaningfully encoded in LLM representations.
Recoverability of DAG structure peaks in intermediate layers.
Recovery varies systematically by node depth, edge span, and model scale.
The framework enables nontrivial recovery of dependency graphs.
Larger models achieve higher recoverability, and reasoning-oriented training recipes provide modest gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on frozen pretrained models; it remains open whether fine-tuning or reinforcement learning alters the internal geometry of reasoning.
The probing approach assumes that reasoning DAG structure is linearly accessible in hidden states; nonlinear or distributed encodings may require more expressive probes.
The DAG formalization for GSM8K relies on GPT-5 mini, which may introduce noise or bias.
future_direction: Extend the framework to dynamic or cyclic reasoning.
Incorporate more expressive probes.
Investigate how training interventions affect internal reasoning structure.
papers.abstract: Recent progress in large language models has renewed interest in mechanistically characterizing how multi-step reasoning is represented and computed. While much prior work treats reasoning as a linear chain of steps, many reasoning problems are more naturally structured as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where intermediate conclusions may depend on multiple premises, branch into parallel sub-derivations, and later merge or be reused. Understanding whether such graph-structured reasoning is reflected in model internals remains an open question. In this work, we introduce Reasoning DAG Probing, a framework that directly asks whether LLM hidden states encode the geometry of a reasoning DAG in a linearly accessible form, and where this structure emerges across layers. Within this framework, we associate each reasoning node with a textual realization and train lightweight probes to predict two graph-theoretic properties from hidden states: node depth and pairwise node distance. We use these probes to analyze the layerwise emergence of DAG structure and evaluate controls that disrupt reasoning-relevant structure while preserving superficial textual properties. Our results provide evidence that reasoning DAG geometry is meaningfully encoded in intermediate layers, with recoverability varying systematically by node depth and model scale, suggesting that LLM reasoning is not only sequential but exhibits measurable internal graph structure.

papers.title: HiCLIP: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining with Hierarchy-aware Attention
papers.research_question: How can we capture the hierarchical nature of semantics in images and texts to improve contrastive vision-language pre-training and cross-modal alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces hierarchy-aware attention into CLIP to explicitly capture hierarchical semantics in images and texts, improving cross-modal alignment and performance on downstream vision and vision-language tasks.
papers.conclusion: HiCLIP effectively captures hierarchical structures in vision and language through hierarchy-aware attention, leading to improved multimodal representations and superior performance on a range of downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
HiCLIP outperforms CLIP and other CLIP-style baselines on visual recognition and vision-language downstream tasks.
The hierarchy-aware attention enables unsupervised induction of hierarchical structures in images and texts that align with human intuition.
Both the Group Transformer (for vision) and Tree Transformer (for language) contribute to the performance gains, with synergy when used together.
HiCLIP shows consistent improvements when scaling pretraining data and model size.
HiCLIP achieves better performance on vision-language tasks than methods relying solely on additional self-supervised objectives.
papers.limitation: The unsupervised hierarchy induction relies on fixed threshold values for splitting, which may not be adaptive to each input image or sentence.
future_direction: Scale up the pretraining dataset and the scale of the visual encoder to fully validate scalability.
Explore better multimodal information fusion operations beyond the simple dot product used in CLIP-style models.
Develop a data-dependent algorithm to parse the attention mask C for each layer adaptively.
papers.abstract: The success of large-scale contrastive vision-language pretraining (CLIP) has benefited both visual recognition and multimodal content understanding. The concise design brings CLIP the advantage in inference efficiency against other vision-language models with heavier cross-attention fusion layers, making it a popular choice for a wide spectrum of downstream tasks. However, CLIP does not explicitly capture the hierarchical nature of high-level and fine-grained semantics conveyed in images and texts, which is arguably critical to vision-language understanding and reasoning. To this end, we equip both the visual and language branches in CLIP with hierarchy-aware attentions, namely Hierarchy-aware CLIP (HiCLIP), to progressively discover semantic hierarchies layer-by-layer from both images and texts in an unsupervised manner. As a result, such hierarchical aggregation significantly improves the cross-modal alignment. To demonstrate the advantages of HiCLIP, we conduct qualitative analysis on its unsupervised hierarchy induction during inference, as well as extensive quantitative experiments on both visual recognition and vision-language downstream tasks.

papers.title: Understanding Chain-of-Thought in Large Language Models via Topological Data Analysis
papers.research_question: Why do different reasoning chains perform differently in reasoning, and what components of reasoning chains play a key role? This paper investigates these questions by analyzing reasoning chains from a structural perspective using topological data analysis.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces topological data analysis to evaluate reasoning chains structurally, finding that greater topological complexity during exploration correlates with higher accuracy, but successful final paths are topologically simpler with fewer redundant cycles.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a structural perspective on reasoning chain quality assessment using topological data analysis and offers guidance for future optimization of reasoning chains.
papers.key_findings:
Under the full-graph view, greater topological complexity (as measured by H0 and H1) correlates with higher accuracy.
Successful reasoning outcomes converge on simpler, more logical paths with reduced redundancy and minimal loops.
GoT (Graph of Thoughts) exhibits the richest topological structure and highest accuracy, while CoT is more linear with fewer loops and lower accuracy.
For the final path, accuracy is negatively correlated with topological complexity, indicating that successful paths are topologically simpler.
