Topological data analysis provides a novel perspective for evaluating reasoning chain quality and reveals structural differences between reasoning paradigms.
papers.abstract: With the development of large language models (LLMs), particularly with the introduction of the long reasoning chain technique, the reasoning ability of LLMs in complex problem-solving has been significantly enhanced. While acknowledging the power of long reasoning chains, we cannot help but wonder: Why do different reasoning chains perform differently in reasoning? What components of the reasoning chains play a key role? Existing studies mainly focus on evaluating reasoning chains from a functional perspective, with little attention paid to their structural mechanisms. To address this gap, this work is the first to analyze and evaluate the quality of the reasoning chain from a structural perspective. We apply persistent homology from Topological Data Analysis (TDA) to map reasoning steps into semantic space, extract topological features, and analyze structural changes. These changes reveal semantic coherence, logical redundancy, and identify logical breaks and gaps. By calculating homology groups, we assess connectivity and redundancy at various scales, using barcode and persistence diagrams to quantify stability and consistency. Our results show that the topological structural complexity of reasoning chains correlates positively with accuracy. More complex chains identify correct answers sooner, while successful reasoning exhibits simpler topologies, reducing redundancy and cycles, enhancing efficiency and interpretability. This work provides a new perspective on reasoning chain quality assessment and offers guidance for future optimization.

papers.title: Abstraction in time: Finding hierarchical linguistic structure in a model of relational processing
papers.research_question: Does the oscillatory activation in LISA/DORA models during processing match human cortical activity during language processing, suggesting a common mechanism for hierarchical representation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LISA/DORA models of relational processing exhibit oscillatory activation patterns during sentence processing that closely match human cortical tracking of hierarchical linguistic structures, suggesting that mechanisms for relational binding may underlie language representation.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that abstract hierarchical linguistic representations can be processed by models of relational reasoning, and suggests that integrating such models with language processing models could advance cognitive modeling.
papers.key_findings:
LISA/DORA models parse English sentences and show firing patterns that mirror cortical activity observed in Ding et al. (2016), with activation bursts at sentence (1Hz), phrasal (2Hz), and syllabic (4Hz) rates.
The models' binding mechanisms, using temporal synchrony and asynchrony, naturally produce hierarchical representations similar to those in human language processing.
These models, built for analogy and relational learning, generalize to language processing without modification, unlike grammar-based or statistical models.
The results support the idea that relational role representation may be a foundation for human cognitive capacities like language.
Integrating models of relational reasoning and language processing could lead to more plausible cognitive models.
future_direction: Testing on natural speech input
Testing on varied syntactic structures
Testing in rich discourse contexts and multilingual input
papers.abstract: Abstract mental representation is fundamental for human cognition. Forming such representations in time, especially from dynamic and noisy perceptual input, is a challenge for any processing modality, but perhaps none so acutely as for language processing. We show that LISA (Hummel & Holyaok, 1997) and DORA (Doumas, Hummel, & Sandhofer, 2008), models built to process and to learn structured (i.e., symbolic) rep resentations of conceptual properties and relations from unstructured inputs, show oscillatory activation during processing that is highly similar to the cortical activity elicited by the linguistic stimuli from Ding et al.(2016). We argue, as Ding et al.(2016), that this activation reflects formation of hierarchical linguistic representation, and furthermore, that the kind of computational mechanisms in LISA/DORA (e.g., temporal binding by systematic asynchrony of firing) may underlie formation of abstract linguistic representations in the human brain. It may be this repurposing that allowed for the generation or mergence of hierarchical linguistic structure, and therefore, human language, from extant cognitive and neural systems. We conclude that models of thinking and reasoning and models of language processing must be integrated —not only for increased plausiblity, but in order to advance both fields towards a larger integrative model of human cognition

papers.title: Probing Graph Representations
papers.research_question: What is encoded in the representations learned by graph-based models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a probing framework to analyze graph representations and shows that transformer-based graph models capture more chemically relevant information compared to message-passing GNNs.
papers.conclusion: Probing is a useful diagnostic tool for understanding and evaluating graph-based models, especially in capturing domain-relevant information.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information in their representations.
Randomly initialized models can also encode useful features, sometimes on par with pretrained models.
Skip connections help preserve information across layers.
Pairwise probing can isolate the effect of specific properties and show causal relationships.
papers.abstract: Today we have a good theoretical understanding of the representational power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). For example, their limitations have been characterized in relation to a hierarchy of Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) isomorphism tests. However, we do not know what is encoded in the learned representations. This is our main question. We answer it using a probing framework to quantify the amount of meaningful information captured in graph representations. Our findings on molecular datasets show the potential of probing for understanding the inductive biases of graph-based models. We compare different families of models and show that transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information compared to models based on message passing. We also study the effect of different design choices such as skip connections and virtual nodes. We advocate for probing as a useful diagnostic tool for evaluating graph-based models.

papers.title: Semantic Relatedness Emerges in Deep Convolutional Neural Networks Designed for Object Recognition
papers.research_question: Whether semantic relatedness among object categories can emerge in deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) without top-down conceptual guidance, purely from perceptual experience during object recognition training.
papers.core_contribution: Semantic relatedness among objects emerges as a by-product of object recognition in DCNNs, without top-down conceptual guidance, and the emerged hierarchical structure is similar to human semantic hierarchy (WordNet).
papers.conclusion: Semantic relatedness of objects can emerge from perceptual experience and task demands without top-down conceptual guidance, suggesting that humans may acquire semantic knowledge in a similar bottom-up manner.
papers.key_findings:
Hierarchical structure of object categories emerges in DCNNs (e.g., AlexNet, VGG, ResNet) trained for object recognition without explicit relation information.
The emerged hierarchical structure is highly similar to human semantic hierarchy (WordNet), with significant correlation.
The hierarchical structure develops in a coarse-to-fine fashion: coarse structure (e.g., living vs. artifact) emerges early, while fine-grained structure within categories develops later.
Object co-occurrence in images is not critical for the emergence of semantic relatedness, as shown by training with single-object images.
Task demands shape the fineness of the hierarchical structure: higher superordinate level classification leads to coarser representations.
papers.limitation:
The finding does not rule out the role of conceptual guidance, as indicated by only moderate correlation between DCNNs and humans.
The DCNNs used are purely feedforward and may not be suitable for studying conceptual guidance; networks with feedback connections or trained with lexical relations are needed.
It is counter-intuitive that semantic relatedness is not derived from object co-occurrence; further studies are needed to examine the hypothesis that shared features drive emergence.
future_direction: Use deep neural networks with feedback connections (e.g., Feedback-CNN or predictive coding network) to understand how conceptual guidance modulates semantic relatedness.
Use networks directly trained with lexical and semantic relations to study the role of conceptual guidance without perceptual experience.
Further studies to examine the hypothesis that features shared by objects, rather than co-appearance frequencies, drive the emergence of semantic relatedness.
papers.abstract: Human not only can effortlessly recognize objects, but also characterize object categories into semantic concepts with a nested hierarchical structure. One dominant view is that top-down conceptual guidance is necessary to form such hierarchy. Here we challenged this idea by examining whether deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) could learn relations among objects purely based on bottom-up perceptual experience of objects through training for object categorization. Specifically, we explored representational similarity among objects in a typical DCNN (e.g., AlexNet), and found that representations of object categories were organized in a hierarchical fashion, suggesting that the relatedness among objects emerged automatically when learning to recognize them. Critically, the emerged relatedness of objects in the DCNN was highly similar to the WordNet in human, implying that top-down conceptual guidance may not be a prerequisite for human learning the relatedness among objects. In addition, the developmental trajectory of the relatedness among objects during training revealed that the hierarchical structure was constructed in a coarse-to-fine fashion, and evolved into maturity before the establishment of object recognition ability. Finally, the fineness of the relatedness was greatly shaped by the demand of tasks that the DCNN performed, as the higher superordinate level of object classification was, the coarser the hierarchical structure of the relatedness emerged. Taken together, our study provides the first empirical evidence that semantic relatedness of objects emerged as a by-product of object recognition in DCNNs, implying that human may acquire semantic knowledge on objects without explicit top-down conceptual guidance.

papers.title: Large Language Models Can Better Understand Knowledge Graphs Than We Thought
papers.research_question: Which input format of knowledge graphs (linearized triples vs. natural language text) is more effective for prompting LLMs to answer fact-intensive questions, and what are the underlying mechanisms and robustness implications?
papers.core_contribution: Linearized triples are more effective than natural language text for prompting LLMs on fact-intensive questions, and larger models are more susceptible to noisy or incomplete knowledge graphs.
papers.conclusion: Linearized triples are more effective for prompting LLMs on fact-intensive questions, and when designing prompt strategies for larger LLMs, the impact of noise in the subgraph should be considered.
papers.key_findings:
When using external knowledge to answer fact-intensive questions, LLMs prefer unordered structural data (linearized triples) over fluent NL text.
Sorting unordered linearized triples may not be necessary, as different LLMs prefer different prompt strategies; researchers need to conduct meticulous experiments to develop more universal KG knowledge injection prompts.
In the input format of linearized triples, LLMs with larger parameters are less robust to such inputs, i.e., they are more susceptible to noisy or incomplete KGs, resulting in performance degradation.
papers.abstract: When we integrate factual knowledge from knowledge graphs (KGs) into large language models (LLMs) to enhance their performance, the cost of injection through training increases with the scale of the models. Consequently, there is significant interest in developing prompt strategies that effectively incorporate KG information into LLMs. However, the community has not yet comprehensively understood how LLMs process and interpret KG information in different input formats and organizations within prompts, and researchers often rely on trial and error. To address this gap, we design extensive experiments to empirically study LLMs' comprehension of different KG prompts. At the literal level, we reveal LLMs' preferences for various input formats (from linearized triples to fluent natural language text). At the attention distribution level, we discuss the underlying mechanisms driving these preferences. We then investigate how the organization of structured knowledge impacts LLMs and evaluate LLMs' robustness in processing and utilizing KG information in practical scenarios. Our experiments show that (1) linearized triples are more effective than fluent NL text in helping LLMs understand KG information and answer fact-intensive questions; (2) Different LLMs exhibit varying preferences for different organizational formats of triples; (3) LLMs with larger scales are more susceptible to noisy, incomplete subgraphs.

papers.title: Emergence of Concepts in DNNs?
papers.research_question: How do existing methods identify concepts in DNNs, and how are conceptual spaces shaped by the tradeoff between predictive accuracy and compression?
papers.core_contribution: Reviews and critiques methods for identifying concepts in DNNs, highlighting limitations due to reliance on partial extensions and the underexplored role of conceptual spaces shaped by accuracy-compression tradeoffs.
papers.conclusion: While DNNs can represent inferential relations between concepts, current methods for identifying these concepts are limited, and understanding holistic conceptual spaces requires new approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Network dissection, feature visualization, and TCAV methods for identifying concepts in DNNs rely on partial extensions or optimization, leading to philosophical issues like indeterminacy of reference.
DNNs can learn concepts shared by multiple predicted classes, indicating representation of non-trivial inferential relations beyond mere extensions.
Conceptual spaces in DNNs are shaped by a tradeoff between predictive accuracy and compression, as illustrated by the Information Bottleneck framework and color naming examples.
Polysemantic neurons suggest that concepts compete for limited representational space, leading to compressed or mixed representations.
Robustness analysis by combining multiple methods could improve reliability, but absolute confirmation of concepts remains challenging.
papers.limitation:
Methods for identifying concepts rely on partial extensions, which underdetermine meaning and face indeterminacy of reference.
Existing methods are limited to extracting local or linear information, not capturing distributed or non-linear representations.
The identification of conceptual spaces and how they arise from accuracy-compression tradeoffs is underexplored.
future_direction: Combining different methods for robustness analysis to increase reliability in concept identification.
Using synthetic datasets with labeled intermediate concepts to test and improve methods for identifying concepts.
Developing methods to understand how entire conceptual spaces are formed holistically in DNNs.
papers.abstract: The present paper reviews and discusses work from computer science that proposes to identify concepts in internal representations (hidden layers) of DNNs. It is examined, first, how existing methods actually identify concepts that are supposedly represented in DNNs. Second, it is discussed how conceptual spaces -- sets of concepts in internal representations -- are shaped by a tradeoff between predictive accuracy and compression. These issues are critically examined by drawing on philosophy. While there is evidence that DNNs able to represent non-trivial inferential relations between concepts, our ability to identify concepts is severely limited.

papers.title: On the Internal Semantics of Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How do time-series foundation models internally represent fundamental time-series concepts? Specifically, which layers encode which concepts, are concept parameters linearly recoverable, how do representations evolve in terms of disentanglement and abstraction across depth, and how do models process compositions of concepts?
papers.core_contribution: A systematic probe-based analysis of time-series foundation models reveals that early layers capture local, time-domain patterns while deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals, and that while atomic concepts are linearly recoverable, representing compositions of concepts remains a challenge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a structured account of TSFM semantics, showing a layered hierarchy of concept learning and highlighting composition as a key limitation for representing interacting temporal phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers mainly capture local, time-domain patterns such as AR(1) coefficient, trend slope, and level shifts.
Deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals (e.g., variance shifts), with representations becoming more disentangled and abstract with depth.
Spectral and time-warping concepts are the least linearly recoverable from model embeddings.
TSFMs exhibit strong linear compositional properties for most concept pairs, but probe performance degrades for composite concepts, revealing interference.
Representations become more organized and linearly recoverable with increased context length in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
While atomic concepts are reliably localized, composition remains a challenge, underscoring a key limitation in current TSFMs’ ability to represent interacting temporal phenomena.
Spectral and time-warping factors are the least linearly accessible.
future_direction: Explore additional TSFMs, multivariate and irregular datasets.
Adopt controlled-capacity non-linear or causal probes.
Investigate architectures and objectives that better linearize phase and time-warping, and non-linear conditional steering.
papers.abstract: Time-series Foundation Models (TSFMs) have recently emerged as a universal paradigm for learning across diverse temporal domains. However, despite their empirical success, the internal mechanisms by which these models represent fundamental time-series concepts remain poorly understood. In this work, we undertake a systematic investigation of concept interpretability in TSFMs. Specifically, we examine: (i) which layers encode which concepts, (ii) whether concept parameters are linearly recoverable, (iii) how representations evolve in terms of concept disentanglement and abstraction across model depth, and (iv) how models process compositions of concepts. We systematically probe these questions using layer-wise analyses, linear recoverability tests, and representation similarity measures, providing a structured account of TSFM semantics. The resulting insights show that early layers mainly capture local, time-domain patterns (e.g., AR(1), level shifts, trends), while deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals, with spectral and warping factors remaining the hardest to recover linearly. In compositional settings, however, probe performance degrades, revealing interference between concepts. This highlights that while atomic concepts are reliably localized, composition remains a challenge, underscoring a key limitation in current TSFMs' ability to represent interacting temporal phenomena.

papers.title: Penzai + Treescope: A Toolkit for Interpreting, Visualizing, and Editing Models As Data
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Penzai, a neural network library that represents models as data structures for easy manipulation, and Treescope, an interactive pretty-printer and visualizer for models and array data.
papers.conclusion: Penzai and Treescope provide a toolkit for interpreting and manipulating models by treating them as data, enabling a wide variety of analyses and interventions without requiring explicit hooks.
papers.abstract: Much of today's machine learning research involves interpreting, modifying or visualizing models after they are trained. I present Penzai, a neural network library designed to simplify model manipulation by representing models as simple data structures, and Treescope, an interactive pretty-printer and array visualizer that can visualize both model inputs/outputs and the models themselves. Penzai models are built using declarative combinators that expose the model forward pass in the structure of the model object itself, and use named axes to ensure each operation is semantically meaningful. With Penzai's tree-editing selector system, users can both insert and replace model components, allowing them to intervene on intermediate values or make other edits to the model structure. Users can then get immediate feedback by visualizing the modified model with Treescope. I describe the motivation and main features of Penzai and Treescope, and discuss how treating the model as data enables a variety of analyses and interventions to be implemented as data-structure transformations, without requiring model designers to add explicit hooks.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: The representational hierarchy in human and artificial visual systems in the presence of object-scene regularities
papers.research_question: Whether deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) approximate human object vision at the behavioral and neural levels, specifically in the context of object-scene regularities.
papers.core_contribution: DCNNs can capture human-like representational hierarchies and conceptual knowledge of object-scene regularities, but the underlying computational strategies differ.
papers.conclusion: DCNNs mimic human vision in capturing object-scene regularities and representational hierarchies, but future models need to consider more diverse training tasks to achieve the rich representational content of the human visual system.
papers.key_findings:
DCNNs in their late processing stages acquire representations that closely capture human conceptual judgments about object-scene co-occurrence.
The representational hierarchy in DCNNs shows similarities with the representational transformations in the human visual pathway, from early visual cortex to frontoparietal areas.
The ability of DCNNs to learn human-like high-level conceptual representations depends on the amount of object-scene co-occurrence in the training set.
Mid/high-level DCNN layers represent the category division for animals and scenes as observed in ventral temporal cortex, but with reduced domain-specific representational richness.
DCNNs and human vision differ in information processing strategies; DCNNs integrate background information in object representations, while human visual cortex separates object and scene processing.
papers.limitation: The dataset used is relatively small compared to typical computer vision datasets, though it is carefully controlled.
future_direction: Develop DCNNs that employ tasks beyond standard object recognition to capture the diverse computational goals of the human visual system.
papers.abstract: Human vision is still largely unexplained. Computer vision made impressive progress on this front, but it is still unclear to which extent artificial neural networks approximate human object vision at the behavioral and neural levels. Here, we investigated whether machine object vision mimics the representational hierarchy of human object vision with an experimental design that allows testing within-domain representations for animals and scenes, as well as across-domain representations reflecting their real-world contextual regularities such as animal-scene pairs that often co-occur in the visual environment. We found that DCNNs trained in object recognition acquire representations, in their late processing stage, that closely capture human conceptual judgements about the co-occurrence of animals and their typical scenes. Likewise, the DCNNs representational hierarchy shows surprising similarities with the representational transformations emerging in domain-specific ventrotemporal areas up to domain-general frontoparietal areas. Despite these remarkable similarities, the underlying information processing differs. The ability of neural networks to learn a human-like high-level conceptual representation of object-scene co-occurrence depends upon the amount of object-scene co-occurrence present in the image set thus highlighting the fundamental role of training history. Further, although mid/high-level DCNN layers represent the category division for animals and scenes as observed in VTC, its information content shows reduced domain-specific representational richness. To conclude, by testing within- and between-domain selectivity while manipulating contextual regularities we reveal unknown similarities and differences in the information processing strategies employed by human and artificial visual systems.

papers.title: Hypernym Bias: Unraveling Deep Classifier Training Dynamics through the Lens of Class Hierarchy
papers.research_question: What patterns do neural networks learn first and last? Specifically, how do hierarchical relationships between classes evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Networks learn hypernyms (higher-level categories) earlier than hyponyms (specific categories) during training, and we introduce a framework to track this hierarchical learning dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Hypernym bias is a consistent phenomenon across architectures and datasets, providing a framework for studying training dynamics and connecting early training bias to neural collapse.
papers.key_findings:
Hypernyms reach near maximum recognition accuracy early in training.
The learned representations align with the semantic structure of the dataset (WordNet).
Neural collapse properties appear earlier in hypernym label spaces.
The phenomenon is consistent across architectures (ResNet, ViT, MobileNet) and datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100, DBPedia).
The training dynamics can be interpreted as top-to-bottom hierarchical label clustering.
papers.limitation:
The hierarchical structure of WordNet is imperfect and may not fully capture class relationships.
The phenomenon is less pronounced in datasets with less defined hierarchies (e.g., CIFAR-100).
future_direction: Extend the notion of hypernym bias to other domains (e.g., AudioSet).
Learn class hierarchies through data-driven hierarchical clustering instead of relying on external structures.
Investigate theoretical connections between hypernym bias and other known biases (e.g., simplicity bias, frequency principle).
papers.abstract: We investigate the training dynamics of deep classifiers by examining how hierarchical relationships between classes evolve during training. Through extensive experiments, we argue that the learning process in classification problems can be understood through the lens of label clustering. Specifically, we observe that networks tend to distinguish higher-level (hypernym) categories in the early stages of training, and learn more specific (hyponym) categories later. We introduce a novel framework to track the evolution of the feature manifold during training, revealing how the hierarchy of class relations emerges and refines across the network layers. Our analysis demonstrates that the learned representations closely align with the semantic structure of the dataset, providing a quantitative description of the clustering process. Notably, we show that in the hypernym label space, certain properties of neural collapse appear earlier than in the hyponym label space, helping to bridge the gap between the initial and terminal phases of learning. We believe our findings offer new insights into the mechanisms driving hierarchical learning in deep networks, paving the way for future advancements in understanding deep learning dynamics.

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: Towards Compositionality in Concept Learning
papers.research_question: How can we automatically discover compositional concept representations from foundation models, given that existing unsupervised concept extraction methods fail to produce composable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Compositional Concept Extraction (CCE), an unsupervised method that enforces orthogonality between concept attributes to extract compositional concept representations from foundation models, improving both compositionality and downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: CCE successfully extracts compositional concept representations from foundation models, addressing the compositionality shortcomings of existing methods and enhancing downstream performance.
papers.key_findings:
Existing unsupervised concept extraction methods (e.g., PCA, ACE, Dictionary Learning) fail to produce compositional concept representations.
Ground-truth concept representations in foundation models (e.g., CLIP) are compositional, exhibiting orthogonality between attributes and non-orthogonality within attributes.
The proposed CCE method enforces these orthogonality properties by construction and extracts more compositional concepts than baselines across image and text datasets.
Concepts extracted by CCE yield better accuracy on downstream classification tasks compared to concepts from baseline methods.
The compositionality of concepts is vital for use cases like model explanation, behavior editing, and few-shot learning.
papers.limitation:
The study assumes concepts are compositional, but real-world concepts can be non-compositional (e.g., 'hot dog').
The concept structure is flat and does not account for hierarchical composition.
Unsupervised concept extraction requires manual inspection to assign names to discovered concepts, which can be labor-intensive.
future_direction: Study of non-compositional concepts.
Study of hierarchical concept structures.
papers.abstract: Concept-based interpretability methods offer a lens into the internals of foundation models by decomposing their embeddings into high-level concepts. These concept representations are most useful when they are compositional, meaning that the individual concepts compose to explain the full sample. We show that existing unsupervised concept extraction methods find concepts which are not compositional. To automatically discover compositional concept representations, we identify two salient properties of such representations, and propose Compositional Concept Extraction (CCE) for finding concepts which obey these properties. We evaluate CCE on five different datasets over image and text data. Our evaluation shows that CCE finds more compositional concept representations than baselines and yields better accuracy on four downstream classification tasks. Code and data are available at https://github.com/adaminsky/compositional_concepts .

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models rely less consistently on the subspace mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies.
Findings are based on a specific reverse dictionary task and may not generalize to all reasoning contexts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit emergent behaviors suggestive of human-like reasoning. While recent work has identified structured, human-like conceptual representations within these models, it remains unclear whether they functionally rely on such representations for reasoning. Here we investigate the internal processing of LLMs during in-context concept inference. Our results reveal a conceptual subspace emerging in middle to late layers, whose representational structure persists across contexts. Using causal mediation analyses, we demonstrate that this subspace is not merely an epiphenomenon but is functionally central to model predictions, establishing its causal role in inference. We further identify a layer-wise progression where attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace, which is subsequently leveraged by later layers to generate predictions. Together, these findings provide evidence that LLMs dynamically construct and use structured, latent representations in context for inference, offering insights into the computational processes underlying flexible adaptation.

papers.title: Classifier with Hierarchical Topographical Maps as Internal\n Representation
papers.research_question: How can hierarchical topographic maps be combined with supervised learning in deep architectures to improve representation and classification, and how does this compare to traditional deep learning approaches?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a hierarchical topographic map architecture that combines bottom-up self-organization with top-down error correction, demonstrating improved clustering and comparable classification performance to multilayer perceptrons.
papers.conclusion: The hierarchical architecture allows for better representation and clustering, and while topographic constraints may seem hindering, they could offer advantages in generalization for specific problem domains.
papers.key_findings:
CRSOM provides better clustering and sparser representations compared to conventional SOM.
Deeper layers in M-rRBF improve class separation and generalization performance.
The generalization performance of rRBF is statistically equivalent to MLP on tested datasets.
Topographic constraints in hidden layers can enhance visualization and potentially robustness.
Context from class labels biases topographic maps to cluster similar classes together.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted on relatively simple datasets, and scalability to larger problems is not yet demonstrated.
The advantage of topographic organization in biological systems is not clear, and it may be a constraint in machine learning.
future_direction: Applying the model to more complicated large-scale benchmarks.
Investigating the advantages of topographic organization in biological systems for machine learning.
papers.abstract:
In this study we want to connect our previously proposed context-relevant
topographical maps with the deep learning community. Our architecture is a
classifier with hidden layers that are hierarchical two-dimensional
topographical maps. These maps differ from the conventional self-organizing
maps in that their organizations are influenced by the context of the data
labels in a top-down manner. In this way bottom-up and top-down learning are
combined in a biologically relevant representational learning setting. Compared
to our previous work, we are here specifically elaborating the model in a more
challenging setting compared to our previous experiments and to advance more
hidden representation layers to bring our discussions into the context of deep
representational learning.

papers.title: Low-Dimensional Structure in the Space of Language Representations is Reflected in Brain Responses
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks? Does the low-dimensional structure of these representations correspond to brain responses during language processing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a low-dimensional structure in the space of language representations and shows that this structure can predict how well each representation maps to human brain responses to natural language, suggesting it captures part of the brain's natural language representation hierarchy.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure in language representations reflects the brain's natural language processing hierarchy, suggesting that the embedding captures some part of the brain's representation structure.
papers.key_findings:
A low-dimensional structure exists in the space of language representations, with the first MDS dimension capturing a progression from word embeddings to syntactic/semantic tasks to next-word embeddings.
The representation embeddings can predict fMRI encoding model performance, indicating a link between the representation space and brain responses.
Projecting the first MDS dimension onto the brain recovers known language processing hierarchies, with early auditory cortex explained by lower-level features and higher-order areas by later layers.
Most pairs of representations can be correctly matched to their brain response patterns using the representation embeddings.
The low-dimensional structure is consistent across different language models and translation models.
papers.limitation: Negative discriminability scores for some representation pairs, possibly due to disconnect between task affinities and brain representations, e.g., for GloVe next-word embedding.
papers.abstract: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks? We answer this question by adapting an encoder-decoder transfer learning method from computer vision to investigate the structure among 100 different feature spaces extracted from hidden representations of various networks trained on language tasks. This method reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and translation models smoothly interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic and semantic tasks, and future word embeddings. We call this low-dimensional structure a language representation embedding because it encodes the relationships between representations needed to process language for a variety of NLP tasks. We find that this representation embedding can predict how well each individual feature space maps to human brain responses to natural language stimuli recorded using fMRI. Additionally, we find that the principal dimension of this structure can be used to create a metric which highlights the brain's natural language processing hierarchy. This suggests that the embedding captures some part of the brain's natural language representation structure.

papers.title: Unit Testing for Concepts in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Whether neural networks are consistent with Fodor's theory of concepts, specifically whether they can be seen as implementing symbolic conceptual representations.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework of unit tests to evaluate if neural networks implement symbolic conceptual representations per Fodor's criteria, finding models succeed on groundedness, modularity, and reusability but fail on causality.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks exhibit grounded behavior and possess modular, context-independent type representations, but lack evidence of a direct causal connection between constituent and composite concepts, a key aspect of Fodor's theory.
papers.key_findings:
Models' predictions are grounded to expected perceptual features, though performance degrades with spurious correlations.
Representations of atomic concepts generalize to unseen compositions, indicating reusable type representations.
Ablating a constituent concept largely preserves other concepts, suggesting modular representations.
No direct causal link found between constituent concept representations and composite concept predictions.
Pretrained models show an inductive bias for shape over color, but pretraining does not consistently improve conceptual structure across tests.
papers.limitation:
INLP ablation only removes linear information, and diagnostic functions are restricted to linear models.
Analysis primarily treats the encode function as a block, not examining internal layers comprehensively.
future_direction: Find alternative implementations of ablate (e.g., using recent methods like Tucker et al. 2021 or Meng et al. 2022).
Expand unit tests to reflect empirical predictions from theories of concept acquisition.
Conduct a complete investigation of internal layers.
papers.abstract: Many complex problems are naturally understood in terms of symbolic concepts. For example, our concept of "cat" is related to our concepts of "ears" and "whiskers" in a non-arbitrary way. Fodor (1998) proposes one theory of concepts, which emphasizes symbolic representations related via constituency structures. Whether neural networks are consistent with such a theory is open for debate. We propose unit tests for evaluating whether a system's behavior is consistent with several key aspects of Fodor's criteria. Using a simple visual concept learning task, we evaluate several modern neural architectures against this specification. We find that models succeed on tests of groundedness, modularlity, and reusability of concepts, but that important questions about causality remain open. Resolving these will require new methods for analyzing models' internal states.

papers.title: From Tokens to Thoughts: How LLMs and Humans Trade Compression for Meaning
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how LLMs and humans balance compression and meaning in conceptual representation, specifically examining the alignment of LLM-emergent categories with human-defined categories, the fidelity to fine-grained semantic structure like typicality, and the differences in compression-meaning trade-off strategies.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs and humans employ different strategies in the compression-meaning trade-off: LLMs achieve broad categorical alignment but optimize for aggressive statistical compression at the cost of semantic nuance, while humans maintain 'inefficient' representations that preserve rich contextual structure. Encoder models surprisingly outperform much larger decoder models in human alignment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs and humans optimize differently for compression versus meaning preservation, with LLMs favoring statistical efficiency and humans favoring adaptive utility. This divergence highlights the need for AI models that preserve conceptual 'inefficiencies' essential for human-like understanding.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs capture broad categorical boundaries aligned with human categories but show weak correlation with fine-grained typicality judgments.
LLMs achieve more optimal information-theoretic compression (lower L objective) than human conceptual structures.
Encoder models (e.g., BERT) match or exceed the human-alignment performance of decoder models 100x larger, indicating distinct representational mechanisms for understanding vs. generation.
Training dynamics analysis of OLMo-7B reveals a two-phase trajectory: rapid initial concept formation followed by architectural reorganization where semantic processing migrates to mid-network layers.
Human categories appear less statistically efficient but are optimized for adaptive flexibility and rich semantic preservation, unlike LLMs which prioritize compression.
papers.limitation:
The metrics used capture information-compression trade-off and geometric efficiency but do not directly measure all aspects of human-style conceptual abstraction or reasoning.
The analysis is limited to open-source models, excluding closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5 and Claude.
future_direction: Incorporate hierarchical and compositional structure to capture nested relationships between categories.
Incorporate feature- and relation-based biases to help models focus on meaningful perceptual or functional attributes.
Incorporate theory- or causally grounded priors to constrain learning and support flexible generalization.
papers.abstract: Humans organize knowledge into compact conceptual categories that balance compression with semantic richness. Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit impressive linguistic abilities, but whether they navigate this same compression-meaning trade-off remains unclear. We apply an Information Bottleneck framework to compare human conceptual structure with embeddings from 40+ LLMs using classic categorization benchmarks. We find that LLMs broadly align with human category boundaries, yet fall short on fine-grained semantic distinctions. Unlike humans, who maintain ``inefficient'' representations that preserve contextual nuance, LLMs aggressively compress, achieving more optimal information-theoretic compression at the cost of semantic richness. Surprisingly, encoder models outperform much larger decoder models in human alignment, suggesting that understanding and generation rely on distinct representational mechanisms. Training-dynamics analysis reveals a two-phase trajectory: rapid initial concept formation followed by architectural reorganization, during which semantic processing migrates from deep to mid-network layers as the model discovers increasingly efficient, sparser encodings. These divergent strategies, where LLMs optimize for compression and humans for adaptive utility, reveal fundamental differences between artificial and natural intelligence. This highlights the need for models that preserve the conceptual ``inefficiencies'' essential for human-like understanding.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Cause and Effect: Hierarchical Concept-based Explanation of Neural\n Networks
papers.research_question: How can we explain neural network decisions based on high-level concepts and quantify causal relationships between concepts and task classes?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for quantifying causal relationships (necessary, sufficient, etc.) between concepts and task classes in neural networks, and constructs a concept hierarchy via decision trees for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively explains neural networks by quantifying causal concept-task relationships and constructing interpretable concept hierarchies, demonstrating improved performance over previous methods.
papers.key_findings:
The method can quantify four types of causal relationships (necessary, sufficient, negative necessary, negative sufficient) between concepts and task classes using an adapted F1 score and AUC.
It uses a non-linear concept classifier with the same structure as the task classifier, initialized with the task classifier's weights, to track concepts across layers.
The concept hierarchy built via decision trees reveals how combinations of concepts lead to task predictions, providing interpretable explanations.
Experiments show the method outperforms TCAV and IBD in identifying relevant concepts and avoiding unreliable ones.
The method is applicable to various network architectures and does not require task training data for explanation.
papers.limitation:
The choice of which layer to inspect is not straightforward; concepts may be present in earlier layers but not in later ones.
The distribution sample set must be representative of likely inputs, otherwise the quantified relationships may be skewed.
papers.abstract:
In many scenarios, human decisions are explained based on some high-level
concepts. In this work, we take a step in the interpretability of neural
networks by examining their internal representation or neuron's activations
against concepts. A concept is characterized by a set of samples that have
specific features in common. We propose a framework to check the existence of a
causal relationship between a concept (or its negation) and task classes. While
the previous methods focus on the importance of a concept to a task class, we
go further and introduce four measures to quantitatively determine the order of
causality. Moreover, we propose a method for constructing a hierarchy of
concepts in the form of a concept-based decision tree which can shed light on
how various concepts interact inside a neural network towards predicting output
classes. Through experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed
method in explaining the causal relationship between a concept and the
predictive behaviour of a neural network as well as determining the
interactions between different concepts through constructing a concept
hierarchy.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways for step-by-step reasoning, with a functional rift in the middle layers where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior, and answer tokens are collected from both the generated CoT and the question context.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning in LLMs is implemented by multiple parallel pathways and a functional rift in the middle layers, with answer tokens collected from various sources.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning.
There is a functional rift in the middle layers (around layer 16 in Llama-2 7B) where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior.
Answer-writing heads appear in the later half of the model (after layer 16).
The model uses both the generated CoT and the question context to generate answers.
Different subtasks (decision, copy, induction) share many of the same attention heads.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Llama-2 7B and the PrOntoQA dataset, which may not generalize to other models or real-world reasoning tasks.
The hydra effect and backup circuits in large models make mechanistic interpretation challenging.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and more diverse reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Generalized Shape Metrics on Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How can we define a rigorous framework of metric spaces to quantify representational dissimilarity across large collections of neural networks, enabling systematic analyses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework of generalized shape metrics that provide a rigorous foundation for comparing neural representations across networks, satisfying metric properties like the triangle inequality and enabling downstream analyses such as clustering and regression.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that generalized shape metrics offer a rigorous and practical framework for comparing neural representations, enabling large-scale analyses and drawing connections to shape analysis literature.
papers.key_findings:
Existing representational similarity measures (CCA, RSA, CKA) can violate the triangle inequality, but can be modified to become proper metrics within the generalized shape framework.
A novel metric for convolutional layers is formulated that respects translation equivariance, distinguishing it from flattened metrics that ignore spatial structure.
The metric spaces on neural representations can be approximated by Euclidean embeddings with low distortion, enabling the use of standard machine learning methods.
In the Allen Brain Observatory, representational similarity predicts the anatomical hierarchy of visual brain regions.
In NAS-Bench-101, representations in early and deep layers show surprising correlations across architectures.
future_direction: Combining generalized shape metrics with other analysis techniques like topological data analysis.
Developing probabilistic versions of generalized shape metrics to handle stochastic representations.
Applying generalized shape metrics to analyze representations in large language models.
papers.abstract: Understanding the operation of biological and artificial networks remains a difficult and important challenge. To identify general principles, researchers are increasingly interested in surveying large collections of networks that are trained on, or biologically adapted to, similar tasks. A standardized set of analysis tools is now needed to identify how network-level covariates-such as architecture, anatomical brain region, and model organism-impact neural representations (hidden layer activations). Here, we provide a rigorous foundation for these analyses by defining a broad family of metric spaces that quantify representational dissimilarity. Using this framework, we modify existing representational similarity measures based on canonical correlation analysis and centered kernel alignment to satisfy the triangle inequality, formulate a novel metric that respects the inductive biases in convolutional layers, and identify approximate Euclidean embeddings that enable network representations to be incorporated into essentially any off-the-shelf machine learning method. We demonstrate these methods on large-scale datasets from biology (Allen Institute Brain Observatory) and deep learning (NAS-Bench-101). In doing so, we identify relationships between neural representations that are interpretable in terms of anatomical features and model performance.

papers.title: Visualisation and 'Diagnostic Classifiers' Reveal how Recurrent and Recursive Neural Networks Process Hierarchical Structure (Extended Abstract)
papers.research_question: How do recurrent neural networks learn and process languages with hierarchical, compositional semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Diagnostic classifiers reveal that gated recurrent neural networks follow a cumulative strategy when processing hierarchical arithmetic expressions, demonstrating the method's utility for interpreting neural network internals.
papers.conclusion: GRUs successfully process hierarchical structure by approximating a cumulative strategy, and diagnostic classifiers are an effective tool for analyzing neural network internal dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
GRUs can learn to compute the meaning of arithmetic expressions and generalize to longer expressions, while SRNs cannot.
Diagnostic classification shows that GRUs implement a strategy similar to the cumulative strategy, not the recursive strategy.
The method provides quantitative insights into network dynamics, overcoming limitations of visualization-based approaches.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate how recurrent neural networks can learn and process languages with hierarchical, compositional semantics. To this end, we define the artificial task of processing nested arithmetic expressions, and study whether different types of neural networks can learn to compute their meaning. We find that simple recurrent networks cannot find a generalising solution to this task, but gated recurrent neural networks perform surprisingly well: networks learn to predict the outcome of the arithmetic expressions with high accuracy, although performance deteriorates somewhat with increasing length. We test multiple hypotheses on the information that is encoded and processed by the networks using a method called diagnostic classification. In this method, simple neural classifiers are used to test sequences of predictions about features of the hidden state representations at each time step. Our results indicate that the networks follow a strategy similar to our hypothesised ‘cumulative strategy’, which explains the high accuracy of the network on novel expressions, the generalisation to longer expressions than seen in training, and the mild deterioration with increasing length. This, in turn, shows that diagnostic classifiers can be a useful technique for opening up the black box of neural networks.

papers.title: Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers: A cross-lingual exploration of knowledge
papers.research_question: This study examines the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and investigates the role of attention mechanisms in this process.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes MEMAT, a knowledge editing method that modifies attention heads in addition to MLP layers, leading to improved performance, cross-lingual portability, and enhanced model understanding of edited facts.
papers.conclusion: MEMAT improves knowledge editing by leveraging attention heads, demonstrating portability and effectiveness across languages, and enhancing the model's understanding of the inserted factual associations.
papers.key_findings:
MEMIT's cross-lingual performance is dependent on subject tokenization similarity between languages.
Attention heads encode language-independent information about factual associations, achieving high accuracy in classifying truthful sentences.
MEMAT outperforms MEMIT across all evaluation metrics (success and magnitude), with improvements exceeding 10% in some cases.
The attention head corrections learned by MEMAT are portable and can be recycled for editing new sets of factual triplets.
MEMAT enhances the model's comprehension of the edited knowledge rather than merely reintroducing it, as evidenced by improved paraphrase and neighborhood metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to English and Catalan; generalization to other linguistic contexts may be limited due to alphabet similarity.
Broader challenges in knowledge editing persist, such as the inability to modify related knowledge and lack of bidirectionality.
future_direction: Investigating language adaptation techniques to enable models to perform tasks in a more language-agnostic manner.
Exploring the role that each architecture component plays in alternative domains to enhance explainable AI.
papers.abstract: Recent research has explored methods for updating and modifying factual knowledge in large language models, often focusing on specific multi-layer perceptron blocks. This study expands on this work by examining the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and delving into the role of attention mechanisms in this process. Drawing from the insights gained, we propose Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers (MEMAT), a method that achieves significant improvements in all metrics while requiring minimal parameter modifications. MEMAT delivers a remarkable 10% increase in magnitude metrics, benefits languages not included in the training data and also demonstrates a high degree of portability. Our code and data are at https://github.com/dtamayo-nlp/MEMAT.

papers.title: Interpretable Image Recognition with Hierarchical Prototypes
papers.research_question: How can we build an interpretable image recognition model that uses hierarchically organized prototypes to classify objects at every level in a predefined taxonomy and also detect novel classes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces HPnet, a model that uses hierarchically organized prototypes to classify images at every level of a taxonomy and detect novel classes, providing interpretable explanations at each level.
papers.conclusion: HPnet is the first CNN-based model to organize prototypes hierarchically and perform novel class detection across taxonomy levels, leading to dramatically improved interpretability while maintaining competitive accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
HPnet performs approximately as well as its black-box counterpart (VGG-16) while providing interpretable classifications.
The model can correctly classify novel data at the coarse level above chance rate.
The learned latent space exhibits good clustering quality, with prototypes surrounded by patch vectors from images of the correct class.
The model provides distinct explanations for predictions at each level of the taxonomy.
The hierarchical prototype approach enables interpretable classification of images from previously unseen classes at the appropriate taxonomic level.
papers.limitation: The interpretability constraints cause a drop in accuracy compared to the black-box model.
papers.abstract: Vision models are interpretable when they classify objects on the basis of features that a person can directly understand. Recently, methods relying on visual feature prototypes have been developed for this purpose. However, in contrast to how humans categorize objects, these approaches have not yet made use of any taxonomical organization of class labels. With such an approach, for instance, we may see why a chimpanzee is classified as a chimpanzee, but not why it was considered to be a primate or even an animal. In this work we introduce a model that uses hierarchically organized prototypes to classify objects at every level in a predefined taxonomy. Hence, we may find distinct explanations for the prediction an image receives at each level of the taxonomy. The hierarchical prototypes enable the model to perform another important task: interpretably classifying images from previously unseen classes at the level of the taxonomy to which they correctly relate, e.g. classifying a hand gun as a weapon, when the only weapons in the training data are rifles. With a subset of ImageNet, we test our model against its counterpart black-box model on two tasks: 1) classification of data from familiar classes, and 2) classification of data from previously unseen classes at the appropriate level in the taxonomy. We find that our model performs approximately as well as its counterpart black-box model while allowing for each classification to be interpreted.

papers.title: A Compositional Neural Architecture for Language
papers.research_question: How can hierarchical structure and compositionality in language be reconciled with principles from cell assembly computation in neuroscience?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a neural architecture based on multidimensional coordinate systems and gain modulation to explain how the brain achieves compositional and hierarchical language processing.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a neural architecture that unifies insights from linguistics, psycholinguistics, and neuroscience to explain how the brain achieves compositional language processing through gain modulation and neural oscillations.
papers.key_findings:
The neural architecture uses a manifold of neural trajectories to encode sensory, motor, and abstract linguistic states.
Gain modulation, including inhibition, tunes the path in the manifold and infers latent structure.
Predictive information about upcoming sensory input during production and comprehension is available without a separate operation.
The architecture synthesizes neural entrainment to speech, systems neuroscience, category theory, and a symbolic-connectionist computational model (DORA) that uses time and rhythm.
The proposal moves toward unifying insights from linguistics and psycholinguistics with neural computation.
papers.abstract: Hierarchical structure and compositionality imbue human language with unparalleled expressive power and set it apart from other perception-action systems. However, neither formal nor neurobiological models account for how these defining computational properties might arise in a physiological system. I attempt to reconcile hierarchy and compositionality with principles from cell assembly computation in neuroscience; the result is an emerging theory of how the brain could convert distributed perceptual representations into hierarchical structures across multiple timescales while representing interpretable incremental stages of (de)compositional meaning. The model's architecture-a multidimensional coordinate system based on neurophysiological models of sensory processing-proposes that a manifold of neural trajectories encodes sensory, motor, and abstract linguistic states. Gain modulation, including inhibition, tunes the path in the manifold in accordance with behavior and is how latent structure is inferred. As a consequence, predictive information about upcoming sensory input during production and comprehension is available without a separate operation. The proposed processing mechanism is synthesized from current models of neural entrainment to speech, concepts from systems neuroscience and category theory, and a symbolic-connectionist computational model that uses time and rhythm to structure information. I build on evidence from cognitive neuroscience and computational modeling that suggests a formal and mechanistic alignment between structure building and neural oscillations, and moves toward unifying basic insights from linguistics and psycholinguistics with the currency of neural computation.

papers.title: Visualisation and 'Diagnostic Classifiers' Reveal How Recurrent and Recursive Neural Networks Process Hierarchical Structure
papers.research_question: How do neural networks learn and process languages with hierarchical, compositional semantics, specifically whether they can compute the meaning of nested arithmetic expressions and how they do so.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces diagnostic classifiers as a method to analyze internal representations of recurrent neural networks and shows that GRUs follow a cumulative strategy for processing hierarchical arithmetic expressions.
papers.conclusion: Diagnostic classifiers can open the black box of neural networks and reveal the strategies they use, with GRUs approximating a cumulative strategy for processing hierarchical structure.
papers.key_findings:
TreeRNNs learn a recursive solution to compute arithmetic expressions and generalize to longer expressions.
GRUs can learn to compute arithmetic expressions and generalize, but performance deteriorates with length.
Diagnostic classifiers reveal that GRUs follow a strategy similar to a cumulative strategy, not a recursive strategy.
The method of diagnostic classifiers is proposed as a scalable way to analyze high-dimensional RNNs.
Visualization techniques like project-sum-squash provide insight into the TreeRNN's composition function.
papers.limitation:
Diagnostic classifiers for gates may require more complex architectures to handle non-linearities.
The analysis is on an idealized task and has not been applied to deeper networks and real-world tasks.
The network's strategy deviates from the perfect cumulative strategy, especially for right-branching expressions.
future_direction: Using diagnostic classifiers for gates with non-linear architectures.
Applying diagnostic classification to higher-dimensional networks and real-world tasks like language modeling and machine translation.
Further research into the reasons for the mismatch between the network's strategy and the cumulative strategy for right-branching expressions.
papers.abstract: We investigate how neural networks can learn and process languages with hierarchical, compositional semantics. To this end, we define the artificial task of processing nested arithmetic expressions, and study whether different types of neural networks can learn to compute their meaning. We find that recursive neural networks can implement a generalising solution to this problem, and we visualise this solution by breaking it up in three steps: project, sum and squash. As a next step, we investigate recurrent neural networks, and show that a gated recurrent unit, that processes its input incrementally, also performs very well on this task: the network learns to predict the outcome of the arithmetic expressions with high accuracy, although performance deteriorates somewhat with increasing length. To develop an understanding of what the recurrent network encodes, visualisation techniques alone do not suffice. Therefore, we develop an approach where we formulate and test multiple hypotheses on the information encoded and processed by the network. For each hypothesis, we derive predictions about features of the hidden state representations at each time step, and train 'diagnostic classifiers' to test those predictions. Our results indicate that the networks follow a strategy similar to our hypothesised 'cumulative strategy', which explains the high accuracy of the network on novel expressions, the generalisation to longer expressions than seen in training, and the mild deterioration with increasing length. This in turn shows that diagnostic classifiers can be a useful technique for opening up the black box of neural networks.
